chapters.title: Book One — The Ingmarssons
paragraphs: A young farmer was plowing his field one summer morning. The sun shone, the grass sparkled with dew, and the air was so light and bracing that words could not describe it. The horses were frisky from the morning air and pulled the plow along as if in play. They moved at a pace quite different from their usual gait. The man had to practically run to keep up with them.

The earth, as it was turned by the plow, lay black and shone with moisture and richness. The man at the plow was happy at the thought of soon being able to sow his rye. "Why do I feel so discouraged at times and find life so hard?" he wondered. "What more does a person need than sunshine and fair weather to be as happy as a child of Heaven?"

A long, rather broad valley stretched before him, with green and yellow grain fields, mowed clover meadows, potato patches in flower, and little fields of flax with their tiny blue blossoms. Great swarms of white butterflies fluttered above. At the very heart of the valley, as if to complete the picture, lay a big old-fashioned farmstead with many gray outhouses and a large red dwelling. Tall, spreading pear trees stood at the gables. A couple of young birches grew by the gate. Great piles of firewood filled the grass-covered yard, and several huge haystacks rose behind the barn. The farmhouse rising above the low fields was as pretty a sight as a ship with masts and sails towering above the broad surface of the sea.

The man at the plow was thinking: "What a farm you've got! Many well-timbered houses, fine cattle and horses, and servants who are good as gold. You're at least as well-off as anyone in these parts. You'll never have to face poverty.

"But it's not poverty I fear," he said, as if answering his own thought. "I would be satisfied if I were only as good a man as my father or my father's father. What could have put such silly nonsense into your head?" he wondered. "A moment ago you were feeling so happy. Consider this one thing: in father's time all the neighbors followed his lead in everything. The morning he began haymaking, they did the same. The day we started plowing the fallow field at the Ingmar Farm, plows went into the earth the length and breadth of the valley. Yet here I've been plowing for two hours and more without anyone having so much as ground a plowshare.

"I believe I have managed this farm as well as anyone who has borne the name of Ingmar Ingmarsson," he mused. "I can get more for my hay than father ever got for his. And I'm not satisfied to let the weed-choked ditches that crossed the farm in his time remain. What's more, no one can say I misuse the woodlands as he did by converting them into burn-beaten land.

"There are times when all this seems hard to bear," said the young man. "I can't always take it as lightly as I do today. When father and grandfather were alive, people used to say the Ingmarssons had been on earth so long that they must know what pleased our Lord. So the people practically begged them to rule the parish. They appointed both parson and sexton. They decided when the river should be dredged and where jails should be built. But no one consults me, and I have no say in anything.

"It's wonderful, all the same, that troubles can be so easily borne on a morning like this. I could almost laugh at them. And yet I fear that things will be worse than ever for me in the fall. If I do what I'm now thinking of doing, neither the parson nor the judge will shake hands with me when we meet at church on a Sunday. That's something they have always done up to now. I could never hope to be made a guardian of the poor, and I couldn't even think of becoming a churchwarden."

Thinking is never so easy as when you follow a plow up a furrow and down again. You are quite alone, and there is nothing to distract you but the crows hopping about picking up worms. The thoughts came to the man as readily as if someone had whispered them into his ear. Only on rare occasions did they come so easily. "It's Big Ingmar I should talk this over with," he murmured. By Big Ingmar he meant his father, who had been dead three years.

"If I only knew the way, I'd go to him," he said, quite pleased at the idea. "I wonder what Big Ingmar would say if some fine day I came wandering up to him? I picture him settled on a big farm with many fields and meadows, a large house and barns galore, with lots of red cattle and not a black one in the herd. I wonder if he has as many as four pairs of horses?" Ingmar kept on raising the old man's standing higher and higher. "And I dare say it's a certainty that he has been chosen to go to the Council. I dare say, too, that he still wears his old gray homespun."

The plowman suddenly stopped in the middle of a furrow and glanced up, laughing. These thoughts amused him greatly. He was so carried away that he hardly knew whether he was still upon earth. It seemed to him that in a flash he had been lifted all the way up to his old father. "Now I seem to be trudging along a road toward a big farmstead. In the yard there is an old man standing among the grain sacks. He wears a gray homespun coat and has a yellow, thin-lipped face. The hair under the cap is white. I walk up to him quite timidly and say: 'Good day, father!' Big Ingmar hardly deigns to glance at me. 'Who are you?' he says, as if he didn't know me. 'My name is Ingmar Ingmarsson. I come from the parish of Dalarna. They used to call me Little Ingmar.'"

"And now as I come into the living room," he went on, "I see many peasants seated on benches along the walls. All have sandy hair, white eyebrows, and thick underlips. They are all of them as like father as one pea is like another. At the sight of so many people I become shy and linger at the door. But father says: 'Come in, come in! There is always room for an Ingmarsson.'"

"Then father looks around and wonders whether he ought to step into the next room. But since it's just me, he walks out into the kitchen instead. There he seats himself in the fireplace, while I sit down on the chopping block.

"'You've got a fine farm here, father,' I say. 'It's not so bad,' says father, 'but how's everything back home?' 'Oh, everything is all right. Last year we got twelve kroner for a ton of hay.' 'What!' says father. 'Are you here to poke fun at me, Little Ingmar?'

"'But with me everything goes wrong,' I say. 'They're forever telling me that you were as wise as our Lord himself, but no one cares a straw for me.' 'Aren't you one of the district councillors?' the old man asks. 'I'm not on the School Board, or in the vestry, nor am I a councillor.' 'What have you done wrong, Little Ingmar?'

"Then I seem to see the old man lower his eyes and sit pondering. After a while he says: 'Ingmar, you ought to marry some nice girl who will make you a good wife.' 'But that's exactly what I can't do, father,' I reply. 'There isn't a farmer in the parish, even among the poor and lowly, who would give his daughter to me.' 'We Ingmarssons have always made good marriages,' says father. 'No one at home wants any dealings with me,' I say, 'because of a wretched affair that happened a few years back.'

"'Well, you see, father, four years ago—the same year I took over the farm—I was courting Brita of Bergskog.' 'Let me see,' says father, 'do any of our folk live at Bergskog?' He seems to have lost all memory of how things are down on earth. 'No, but they are well-to-do people, and you thought highly of the girl's father.' 'What came of it, then?' 'She accepted me.'"

"Now both father and I are silent a moment. Then the old man continues: 'She was good-looking, of course?' 'Yes,' I reply. 'She had dark hair and bright eyes and rosy cheeks. And she was clever, too, so that mother was pleased with my choice. All might have turned out well, but the mistake was that she didn't want me.' 'She didn't want you?' 'No.'"

"'Oh, no! She was anything but glad. All the same, the banns were published and the wedding day was fixed. So Brita came down to the Ingmar Farm to help mother. I should say, mother is getting old and feeble.' 'I see nothing wrong in all that, Little Ingmar,' says father, as if to cheer me up.

"'But that year nothing seemed to thrive on the farm. The potato crop was a failure, and the cows got sick. So mother and I decided it was best to put off the wedding a year. I thought it didn't matter so much about the wedding as long as the banns had been read. But perhaps it was old-fashioned of me to think that way. In any case, it seems I should not have put it off.'"

"'Had you chosen one of our kind she would have been patient,' says father. 'Well, yes,' I say. 'I could see that Brita didn't like the idea of a postponement. But I felt I couldn't afford a wedding just then. There had been the funeral in the spring, and we didn't want to take on any debt.' 'That was right, Little Ingmar,' says father."

"'Every day Brita became more quiet and strange. I used to wonder what was wrong with her and figured she was homesick, for she had always loved her home and her parents. This will blow over, I thought, when she gets used to us. She'll soon feel at home on the Ingmar Farm. I put up with it all through the summer and fall, but one day I said that I thought it would be best for us to part. Then she cried and begged me not to send her away, so I let things go on as before.'"

The plowman walked along, his lips moving the whole time. He actually imagined that he saw his father's face before him. "I shall have to lay the whole case before the old man, frankly and clearly," he told himself, "so he can advise me."

"'Winter had come and gone, yet nothing was changed. I felt at times that if Brita were going to keep being unhappy, I might better give her up and send her home. However, it was too late to think of that. Then, one evening early in May, we discovered that she had quietly slipped away. We searched for her all night and found her in the morning, lying in the woods a long way from home.'"

"I find it hard now to continue, and take refuge in silence. Then father exclaims: 'In God's name, she wasn't dead, was she?' 'No, not she,' I say, and father notes the tremor in my voice. 'Was the child born?' asks father. 'Yes,' I reply, 'and she had strangled it. It was lying dead beside her.' 'But little Ingmar,' says father, 'surely you didn't let the law take its course?' 'Yes, I reported it to the sheriff,' I say, 'and she was arrested and charged with murder.'"

"Now that father seems to side with me, I say: 'There are many who think I should have managed it so that no one would have known the child was born dead.' 'Why shouldn't she take her punishment?' says father. 'They say if this had happened in your time, you would have made the sheriff believe it was an accident.' 'They're probably right about that,' says father, 'for I was a good man to deal with. But since you didn't see the way out, it was only right to let things take their course. I'm well satisfied with you, Little Ingmar.' Father keeps nodding and nodding, and while he has been talking some of the old Ingmars have come out into the kitchen and are also nodding approvingly. 'Quite right, Little Ingmar, quite right,' they say, for they are folk who have always dealt justly and walked in the ways of God. But then I say to father: 'All the same, I can't help thinking that maybe there was something I could have done to keep the whole thing from happening.' Father grows serious, and the other Ingmars stop nodding."
"The old man sits quite still and does not answer.

"'The last time I saw her was in the courtroom. She was so gentle then, and longed so for her child. Not one harsh word did she say against me. She took all the blame herself. Many in that courtroom were moved to tears, and the judge himself had to swallow hard. He didn't give her more than three years. I guess he saw that she had been driven to it.'"
"But father does not say a word.

"'It will be hard for her when fall comes and she's sent home. They won't be glad to have her back at Bergskog. Her folks all feel she has brought shame upon them, and they're sure to let her know it. There will be nothing for her but to sit at home. She won't even dare go to church. She might end up losing her mind if things go on like that. Brita is not the kind to bear disgrace.'"
"But father doesn't answer.

"'It is not an easy thing for me to marry her! To have a wife that menservants and maidservants will look down upon is not a pleasant prospect for a man with a big farmstead. Nor would mother like it. We never invite people to the house, either for weddings or funerals.'"
"Meanwhile, not a word out of father.

"'Of course at the trial I tried to help her as much as I could. I told the judge that I was entirely to blame, since I took the girl against her will. I also said I considered her so innocent of any wrong that I would marry her then and there, if she could only think better of me. I said that so the sentence wouldn't be too hard. And it was at the trial, as I sat looking at Brita, that I felt it was my duty to stand by her. I said to myself: You'll marry her when she comes out of prison.'"
"Father sits and ponders, but he doesn't speak.

"'I know that this is simply looking at the thing from a human viewpoint, and we Ingmars have always wanted to stand well in the sight of God. Yet sometimes I think that maybe our Lord wouldn't like it if we honored a murderess.'"
"And father doesn't utter a sound.
"'Think, father, how a person must feel who lets another suffer without giving a helping hand. I have been through too much these last few years not to try to do something for her when she gets out.
"Father sits there immovable.

"'Now I can hardly keep back the tears. 'You see, father, I'm a young man and will lose much if I marry her. Everyone seems to think I've already made a mess of my life. They will think still worse of me after this!'"
"But I can't make father say a word.

"'I have often wondered why it is that we Ingmars have been allowed to remain on our farm for hundreds of years, while other farms have all changed hands. And the thought comes to me that perhaps it's because the Ingmars have always tried to walk in the ways of God. We Ingmars need not fear man. We only need to consider whether what we do is the will of God.'"
"Then the old man looks up and says: 'This is a difficult problem, my son. I think I'll go in and talk it over with the other Ingmarssons.'"

"So father goes back to the living room, while I remain in the kitchen. There I sit waiting and waiting, but father does not return. Then, after hours and hours, I get cross and go to him. 'You must have patience, Little Ingmar,' says father. 'This is a difficult question.' And I see all the Ingmars sitting around deliberating; but I can't get them to say a single word."

Smiling, he followed the plow, which was now moving along very slowly. The horses seemed tired and could scarcely drag it. When he came to the end of the furrow, he pulled up the plow and rested. He had become very serious.

"Strange—when you ask someone's advice, you see yourself what is right. Even while you are asking, you discover all at once what you couldn't find out in three whole years. Now it shall be as God wills."
He felt this thing must be done, but at the same time it seemed so hard that the mere thought of it took away his courage. "Help me, Lord!" he said.

Ingmar Ingmarsson was not, however, the only person abroad at that hour. An old man came trudging along the winding path that crossed the fields. It was not difficult to guess his occupation, for he carried on his shoulder a long-handled paintbrush and was spattered with red paint from his cap to his shoes. He stopped a moment at the top of the hill and looked about. He was evidently looking for work. There was a rumor that a great farmhouse in the parish was to be painted that year, and the old painter was going from farm to farm in search of the house.

A little farther on he came upon a man plowing. "Why, there's a farmer who belongs here and knows this neighborhood," thought the painter. "He can tell me all I need to know about that house." So he crossed the path into the field, stepped up to Ingmar, and asked him if he knew where the house was that was to be painted this year.
Ingmar Ingmarsson was startled and stood staring at the man as though he were a ghost.

"Lord, as I live, it's a painter!" he said to himself. "And to think of his coming just now!" He was so dumbfounded that he could not answer the man. He distinctly recalled that every time anyone had said to his father, "You ought to have that big, ugly house of yours painted, Father Ingmar," the old man had always answered: "It shall be painted the year Ingmar marries."
The painter put the question a second time, and a third, but Ingmar stood there, dazed, as if he had not understood him.
"Are they ready at last with their answer?" he wondered. "Is this a message from father to say he wishes me to marry this year?"
He was so overwhelmed by the thought that he hired the man on the spot. Then he went on with his plowing, deeply moved and almost happy.
"You'll see it won't be so hard to do this, now that you know for certain it's father's wish," he said.
II

A fortnight later Ingmar Ingmarsson stood polishing some harness. He seemed to be in a bad mood and found the work rather tiresome. "If I were in our Lord's place," he thought, then put in another rub or two and began again: "If I were in our Lord's place, I'd see to it that a thing was done the instant you had made up your mind to do it. But first the house has to be painted. And you've got to take a trip to town and buy new furniture. And then the banns have to be read three times. So the whole summer goes by before you can do anything. If I were in our Lord's place, I would not put a man's courage to such a long test." He rubbed away at the harness until it shone. "I only know that if I were in our Lord's place, I would help poor men who are willing to do what is right. I wouldn't try their patience."

He caught the sound of wagon wheels from the road and looked out. He knew at once whose rig it was. "The senator from Bergskog is coming!" he shouted into the kitchen, where his mother was at work. Instantly fresh wood was laid on the fire and the coffee mill was set going.

The senator drove into the yard and pulled up without getting out. "No, I'm not going into the house," he said. "I only want a word or two with you, Ingmar. I'm rather pressed for time, as I'm due at the parish meeting."
"Mother is just making some fresh coffee," said Ingmar.
"Thank you, but I must not be late."
"It's been a good while since you were here, Senator," said Ingmar pressingly.
Then Ingmar's mother appeared in the doorway and protested:
"Surely you're not thinking of going without first coming in for a drop of coffee?"
Ingmar unbuttoned the carriage apron, and the senator began to move. "Seeing it's Mother Martha herself who commands me, I suppose I shall have to obey," he said.

The senator was a tall man of striking appearance, with a certain ease of manner. He was of a totally different stamp from Ingmar or his mother, who were very plain looking, with sleepy faces and clumsy bodies. But all the same, the senator had a profound respect for the old Ingmar family. He would gladly have sacrificed his own impressive bearing to be like Ingmar and to become one of the Ingmarssons.
After a while, when Mother Martha had brought the coffee, he began to state his errand.

"I thought," he said, and cleared his throat, "I thought you had best be told what we intend to do with Brita." The cup that Mother Martha held in her hand shook a little, and the teaspoon rattled in the saucer. Then there was a painful silence. "We have been thinking that the best thing would be to send her to America." He made another pause, only to be met by the same ominous silence. He went on: "If she goes to America nobody will know what she has done. She can start a new life over there and, when she has been gone awhile, no one here will remember what happened."
"She will come home first, of course," said Ingmar.
"No; what would she be doing there?"
Again Ingmar was silent. He sat with his eyes nearly closed, as if he were half asleep.
Then Mother Martha took a turn at asking questions. "She'll be needing clothes, won't she?"
"All that has been taken care of. There is a trunk, ready packed, at Loevberg's place, where we always stop when we come to town."
"Her mother will be there to meet her, I suppose?"
"Well, no. She would like to, but I think it's best that they be spared a meeting."
"Maybe so."

"The ticket and some money are waiting for her at Loevberg's, so she will have everything she needs. I felt that Ingmar ought to know of it, so he won't have this burden on his mind any longer," said the senator.
Then Mother Martha kept still, too. Her headkerchief had slipped back, and she sat gazing down at her apron.
"Ingmar should be looking about for a new wife."
Both mother and son stubbornly held their peace.

"Mother Martha needs a helper in this big household. Ingmar should see to it that she has some comfort in her old age." The senator paused a moment, wondering if they could have heard him. "My wife and I wanted to make everything right again," he declared finally.

In the meantime, a sense of great relief had come to Ingmar. Brita was going to America, and he would not have to marry her. After all, a murderess was not to become the mistress of the old Ingmar home. He had kept still, thinking it was not the thing to show at once how pleased he was. But now he began to feel it would be only right for him to say something.
The senator quietly bided his time. He knew he had to give these old-fashioned people time to consider. Presently Ingmar's mother said:

"Brita has paid her penalty; now it's our turn." By this the old woman meant that if the senator wanted any help from the Ingmarssons in return for his having smoothed the way for them, they would not withhold it. But Ingmar took her words differently. He gave a start, as if suddenly wakened from sleep. "What would father say about this?" he wondered. "If I were to lay the whole matter before him again—would he say it's right to let the senator do this? Would father think it proper for an Ingmarsson to let others bear his burden and clean up his mess?"

"I truly believe the old man is keeping close watch of me in this matter," he thought. "He must have sent Brita's father here to show me how mean it is to try to shift everything onto her, poor girl! I bet he noticed I haven't had much desire to make that journey these last few days."
Ingmar got up, poured some brandy into his coffee, and raised the cup.
"Here's a thank you to the senator for coming here today," he said, and clinked cups with him.
III
Ingmar had been busy all morning working around the birches down by the gate. First he had put up a scaffolding, then he had bent the tops of the trees toward each other so that they formed an arch.
"What's all that for?" asked Mother Martha.
"Oh, it suits my fancy to have them grow that way for a change," said Ingmar.

Along came the noon hour, and the menfolk stopped their work. After the midday meal the farmhands went out into the yard and lay down in the grass to sleep. Ingmar Ingmarsson slept too, but he was lying in a broad bed in the chamber off the living room. The only person not asleep was the old mistress, who sat in the big room, knitting.

The door to the entrance hall was cautiously opened, and in came an old woman carrying two large baskets on a yoke. After greeting the mistress, she sat down on a chair by the door and took the lids off the baskets. One was filled with rusks and buns, the other with newly baked loaves of spiced bread. The housewife went over to the old woman at once and began to bargain. Ordinarily she would not have bought a thing, being so used to baking her own bread that she disliked even the smell of bakers' bread. But today it was different, and Mother Martha not only bought a lot of baked goods, but she also ordered cakes and cookies.

While selecting her cakes she began to chat with the old woman, who, like most people that go from place to place and know many folk, was a ready talker. "Kaisa, you're a sensible person," said Mother Martha, "and one can rely on you."
"Yes, indeed," said the other. "If I didn't know enough to keep quiet about most of the things I hear, there'd be some fine hair-pulling matches, I'm thinking!"
"But sometimes you are altogether too close-mouthed, Kaisa."
The old woman looked up. The meaning was quite plain to her.
"May the Lord forgive me!" she said tearfully. "But I talked to the senator's wife at Bergskog when I should have come straight to you."
"So you have been talking to the senator's wife!" And the emphasis given to the last two words spoke volumes.

Ingmar had been startled from his sleep by the opening of the outside door. No one had come in, apparently; still the door stood ajar. He did not know whether it had sprung open or someone had opened it. Too sleepy to get up, he settled back in bed. And then he heard talking in the outer room.
"Now tell me, Kaisa, what makes you think that Brita doesn't care for Ingmar."
"From the very start folks have been saying that her parents made her take him," the old woman answered evasively.
"Speak right out, Kaisa. When I question you, you don't have to beat about the bush. I think I'm able to bear anything you may have to tell me."

"I must say that every time I was at Bergskog, Brita always looked as if she'd been crying. Once, when she and I were alone in the kitchen, I said to her: 'It's a fine husband you'll be getting, Brita.' She looked at me as if she thought I was making fun of her. Then she came out with this: 'You may well say it, Kaisa. Fine, indeed!' She said it in such a way that I seemed to see Ingmar Ingmarsson before me, with his small eyes, and his big red nose, and his fat underlip, and his whole heavy person. It was not a good picture, Mother Martha; but seeing you asked, I had to tell you."
Ingmar could hear every word that was spoken from his bedroom.

"Mother is doing this on purpose," he thought. "She's been wondering about that trip to town tomorrow. Mother thinks I'm going to fetch Brita and bring her home. She doesn't suspect that I'm too big a coward to do it."

"The next time I saw Brita," the old woman went on, "was after she had come here to live with you. I couldn't ask her just then how she liked it here, seeing the house was full of visitors. But when I had gone a ways into the grove, she came running after me.
"'Kaisa!' she called. 'Have you been up at Bergskog lately?'
"'I was there day before yesterday,' I replied.

"'Gracious me! Were you there day before yesterday? And I feel as if I haven't been home in years!' It wasn't easy to know what to say to her, for she looked as if she couldn't bear the least little thing and would cry at whatever I might say. 'You can surely go home for a visit?' I said. 'No, I don't think I shall ever go home again.' 'Oh, do go,' I urged. 'It's beautiful up there now.' 'No, I'll never see the place again,' she said, and looked as if she might collapse."

"I was just about to go on my way when it occurred to me to ask her where the wedding was going to be held—here or at her home. 'We're thinking of having it here, where there is plenty of room.' 'Then see to it that the wedding day isn't put off too long,' I warned. 'We are to be married in a month,' she answered."

"But before Brita and I parted company, it struck me that the Ingmarssons had had a poor harvest. So I said it was not likely they would have a wedding that year. 'In that case I shall have to jump into the river,' she declared."

"A month later I was told the wedding had been put off. Fearing that this would not end well, I went straight to Bergskog and had a talk with Brita's mother. 'They are certainly making a stupid blunder down at the Ingmar Farm,' I told her. 'We are satisfied with their way of doing things,' she said. 'Every day we thank God that our daughter has been so well provided for.'"

"Mother needn't have given herself all this trouble," Ingmar was thinking, "for no one from this farm is going to fetch Brita. There was no reason for her being so upset at the sight of the arch. That is only one of those things a man does so that he can turn to our Lord and say: 'I wanted to do it. Surely you can see that I meant to do it.' But doing it is another matter."

"The last time I saw Brita," Kaisa went on, "was in the middle of winter after a big snowfall. I had come to a narrow path in the wild forest where the walking was heavy. Soon I came upon someone who was sitting in the snow, resting. It was Brita. 'Are you all by yourself up here?' I asked. 'Yes, I'm out for a walk,' she said. I stood stock-still and stared at her. I couldn't imagine what she was doing up there in the forest, so far from home."

"'Yes,' she said. 'If I could only find a hill that was high and steep, I'd certainly throw myself down.' 'You ought to be ashamed to talk like that, and you so well cared for.' 'You see, Kaisa, I'm a bad lot.' 'I'm afraid you are.' 'I am likely to do something dreadful, so I might better be dead.' 'That's only silly talk, child.' 'I turned bad as soon as I went to live with those people.'"

"All at once she began to cry. Then, after a little, she became very meek and said she had suffered so from the bad thoughts that came to her. I walked home with her, and as we parted, she promised me she would do nothing rash if I would only keep quiet about it."
"Still I couldn't help thinking that I ought to talk to someone about this," said Kaisa. "But to whom? I felt awkward about going to important folk like yourselves—"

Just then the bell above the stable rang. The midday rest was over. Mother Martha suddenly interrupted the old woman: "I say, Kaisa, do you think things can ever be right again between Ingmar and Brita?"
"What?" gasped the old woman in astonishment.
"I mean, if by chance she were not going to America, do you suppose she would have him?"
"Well, I should say not!"
"Then you are quite sure she would turn him down."
"Of course she would."
Ingmar sat on the edge of the bed, his legs dangling over the side.

"Now you got just what you needed, Ingmar," he thought. "And now I expect you'll make that journey tomorrow," he said, pounding the edge of the bed with his fist. "How can mother think she'll get me to stay home by showing me that Brita doesn't like me!"
He kept pounding the side of the bed, as if in his mind he were knocking down something that was resisting him.
"Anyway, I'm going to try once more," he decided. "We Ingmars start all over again when things go wrong. No man who is a man can sit back calmly and let a woman fret herself insane over his actions."
Never had he felt so keenly his utter defeat, and he was determined to put himself right.
"I'd be a hell of a man if I couldn't make Brita happy here!" he said.
He dealt the bedpost a last blow before getting up to go back to his work.
"As sure as you're born, it was Big Ingmar who sent old Kaisa here, to make me take that trip to the city."
IV

Ingmar Ingmarsson had arrived in the city and was walking slowly toward the big prison, which was beautifully situated on the crest of a hill overlooking the public park. He did not glance about him but went with eyes downcast, dragging himself along as if he were some feeble old man. He had left off his usual peasant clothes on this occasion and was wearing a black cloth suit and a starched shirt that he had already crumpled. He felt very solemn, yet anxious and reluctant the whole time.
Coming to the graveled yard in front of the jail, he saw a guard on duty and asked him if this was the day Brita Ericsson was to be discharged.
"Yes, I think there is a woman coming out today," the guard answered.
"One who has been in for infanticide," Ingmar explained.
"Oh, that one! Yes, she'll be out this morning."

Ingmar stationed himself under a tree to wait. Not for a second did he take his eyes off the prison gate. "I dare say there are some who have gone in there and haven't fared any too well," he thought. "I don't want to brag, but maybe many on the inside have suffered less than I who am outside. Well, I declare, Big Ingmar has brought me here to fetch my bride from the prison house," he said to himself. "But I can't say that Little Ingmar is overjoyed at the thought. He would have liked seeing her pass through a gate of honor instead, with her mother standing by her side to give her to the bridegroom. And then they should have driven to the church in a flower-trimmed carriage, followed by a big bridal procession. She should have sat beside him dressed as a bride, smiling under her bridal crown."

The gate opened several times. First a chaplain came out, then the wife of the prison governor, and then some servants going to town. Finally Brita came. When the gate opened he felt a cramp at his heart. "It is she," he thought. His eyes dropped. He was paralyzed and could not move. When he had recovered himself, he looked up. She was standing on the steps outside the gate.

She stood there a moment, quite still. She had pushed back her headshawl and, with eyes that were clear and open, she looked out across the landscape. The prison stood on high ground, and beyond the town and the stretches of forest she could see her native hills.
Suddenly she seemed shaken by some unseen force. She covered her face with her hands and sank down upon the stone step. Ingmar could hear her sobs from where he stood.
He went over to her presently and waited. She was crying so hard that she seemed deaf to every other sound. He had to stand there a long time. At last he said:
"Don't cry like that, Brita!"
She looked up. "O God in Heaven!" she exclaimed. "Are you here?"
Instantly all that she had done to him flashed across her mind—and what it must have cost him to come. With a cry of joy she threw her arms around his neck and began to sob again.
"How I have longed for you to come!" she said.
Ingmar's heart began to beat faster at the thought of her being so pleased to see him. "Why, Brita, have you really been longing for me?" he said, quite moved.
"I have wanted so much to ask your forgiveness."
Ingmar drew himself up to his full height and said very coldly:
"There will be plenty of time for that. I don't think we ought to stay here any longer."
"No, this is no place to stay," she answered meekly.
"I have put up at Loevberg's," he said as they walked along the road.
"That's where my trunk is."
"I have seen it there," said Ingmar. "It's too big for the back of the cart, so it will have to be left there till we can send for it."
Brita stopped and looked up at him. This was the first time he had suggested that he meant to take her home.
"I had a letter from father today. He says you also think I ought to go to America."
"I thought there was no harm in having a second choice. It wasn't so certain you would care to come back with me."

She noticed he said nothing about wanting her to come, but perhaps it was because he did not wish to force himself upon her a second time. She grew reluctant. It couldn't be an enviable task to take someone like her to the Ingmar Farm. Then something seemed to say:

"Tell him you will go to America. It is the only service you can do for him. Tell him that, tell him that!" urged something within her. And while this thought was still in her mind, she heard someone say: "I'm afraid I'm not strong enough to go to America. They tell me you have to work very hard over there." It was as if another had spoken, not she herself.
"So they say," Ingmar said indifferently.

She was ashamed of her weakness. That very morning she had told the prison chaplain she was going out into the world a new and better woman. Thoroughly displeased with herself, she walked in silence for some time, wondering how to take back her words. But as soon as she tried to speak, she was held back by the thought that if he still cared for her, it would be the basest ingratitude to push him away again. "If I could only read his thoughts!" she said to herself.

She stopped and leaned against a wall. "All this noise and the sight of so many people makes my head spin," she said. He put out his hand, which she took. Then they went along hand in hand. Ingmar was thinking, "Now we look like sweethearts." All the same, he wondered how it would be when he got home—how his mother and the rest of the folk would take it.

When they came to Loevberg's place, Ingmar said his horse was now thoroughly rested, and if she had no objection they might as well cover the first few miles that day. She thought: "Now is the time to tell him you won't go. Thank him first, then tell him you don't want to go with him." She prayed God she might be shown whether he had come for her only out of pity. Meanwhile, Ingmar had drawn the cart out of the shed. The cart had been newly painted, the dashboard shone, and the cushions had fresh covers. Attached to the buckboard was a little half-withered bouquet of wildflowers. The sight of the flowers made her pause and think. Ingmar had gone back to the stable to harness the horse and was now leading him out. Then she discovered another bouquet between the harness and began to feel that after all he must like her. So it seemed best not to say anything. Otherwise he might think her ungrateful—that she did not understand how big a thing he was offering her.

For a time they drove along without a word. Then, to break the silence, she began questioning him about various things at home. With every question he was reminded of someone whose judgment he feared. How so-and-so will wonder, and how so-and-so will laugh at me, he thought.
He answered only in monosyllables. Time and again she felt like begging him to turn back. "He doesn't want me," she thought. "He doesn't care for me. He is doing this only out of charity."

She soon stopped asking questions. They drove on for miles in deep silence. When they came to their first stopping place, an inn, there were coffee and hot biscuits ready for them. On the tray were some more flowers. She knew then that he had ordered this the day before, when passing through. Was that, too, done only out of kindness and pity? Was he happy yesterday? Was it only today that he had lost heart, after seeing her come out of prison? Tomorrow, when he had forgotten this, perhaps all would be well again.
Sorrow and remorse had softened Brita. She did not want to cause him any more unhappiness. Perhaps, after all, he really—

They stayed at the inn overnight and left early the next morning. By ten o'clock they were already within sight of their parish church. As they drove along the road leading to the church, it was thronged with people, and the bells were ringing.

"Why, it's Sunday!" Brita exclaimed, folding her hands instinctively. She forgot everything else in the thought of going to church and praising God. She wanted to begin her new life with a service in the old church.

"I should love to go to church," she said to Ingmar, never thinking that it might be embarrassing for him to be seen there with her. She was all devotion and gratitude! Ingmar's first impulse was to say she couldn't. He felt he did not have the courage to face the curious glances and gossiping tongues of these people. "It has to be met sooner or later," he thought. "Putting it off won't make it any easier."

He turned and drove onto the church grounds. The service had not yet started, and many people were sitting in the grass and on the stone wall, watching the arrivals. The instant they saw Ingmar and Brita they began to nudge each other, whisper, and point. Ingmar glanced at Brita. She sat with clasped hands, quite unaware of the stir around her. She saw no one, apparently, but Ingmar saw them only too well. They came running after the wagon and did not wonder at their running or their stares. They must have thought their eyes were deceiving them. Of course they could not believe he had come to the house of God with her—the woman who had strangled his child. "This is too much!" he said. "I can't stand it."
"I think you'd better go inside at once, Brita," he suggested.
"Why, certainly," she answered. Attending the service was her only thought. She had not come there to meet people.

Ingmar took his time unharnessing and feeding the horse. Many eyes were fixed upon him, but nobody spoke to him. By the time he was ready to go into the church, most people were already in their pews and the opening hymn was being sung. Walking down the center aisle, he glanced over at the side where the women sat. All the pews were filled except one, and in that there was only one person. He saw at once that it was Brita and knew, of course, that no one had cared to sit with her. Ingmar went and sat down beside her. Brita looked up at him in wonder. She had not noticed before, but now she understood why she had the pew to herself. Then the deep feeling of devotion she had just experienced was swept away by black despair. "How would it all end?" she wondered. She should never have come with him.

Her eyes began to fill. To keep from breaking down she took up an old prayer book from the shelf in front of her and opened it. She kept turning the pages without being able to see a word for the tears. Suddenly something bright caught her eye. It was a bookmark with a red heart, lying between the leaves. She took it out and slipped it toward Ingmar. She saw him close his big hand over it and steal a glance at it. Shortly afterward it lay upon the floor. "What is to become of us?" thought Brita, sobbing behind the prayer book.

As soon as the preacher had stepped down from the pulpit, they went out. Ingmar hurriedly hitched up the horse with Brita's help. By the time the benediction was pronounced and the congregation was filing out, Brita and Ingmar were already off. Both seemed to be thinking the same thought: one who has committed such a crime cannot live among people. They felt as if they had been doing penance by appearing at church. "Neither of us will be able to stand it," they thought.

In the midst of her distress, Brita caught a glimpse of the Ingmar Farm and hardly recognized it. It looked so bright and red. She remembered hearing that the house was to be painted the year Ingmar married. Before, the wedding had been put off because he felt he could not afford the expense. Now she understood that he had always meant to have everything right, but the way had been made rather hard for him.

When they arrived at the farm, the folks were at dinner. "Here comes the boss," said one of the men, looking out. Mother Martha got up from the table, scarcely lifting her heavy eyelids. "Stay where you are, all of you!" she commanded. "No one need rise from the table."

The old woman walked heavily across the room. Those who turned to look after her noticed she had on her best dress, with her silk shawl across her shoulders and her silk kerchief on her head, as if to emphasize her authority. When the horse stopped, she was already at the door.
Ingmar jumped down at once, but Brita kept her seat. He went over to her side and unfastened the carriage apron.
"Aren't you going to get out?" he said.
"No," she replied, then covered her face with her hands and burst into tears.
"I ought never to have come back," she sobbed.
"Oh, do get down!" he urged.
"Let me go back to the city. I'm not good enough for you."
Ingmar thought maybe she was right, but said nothing. He stood with his hand on the apron and waited.
"What does she say?" asked Mother Martha from the doorway.
"She says she isn't good enough for us," Ingmar replied, for Brita's words could scarcely be heard through her sobs.
"What is she crying about?" asked the old woman.
"Because I am such a miserable sinner," said Brita, pressing her hands to her heart, which she thought would break.
"What's that?" the old woman asked once more.
"She says she is such a miserable sinner," Ingmar repeated.

When Brita heard him repeat her words in a cold and indifferent tone, the truth suddenly flashed upon her. No, he could never have stood there and repeated those words to his mother had he been fond of her, or had there been a spark of love in his heart for her.
"Why doesn't she get down?" the old woman then asked.
Suppressing her sobs, Brita spoke up: "Because I don't want to bring misfortune upon Ingmar."

"I think she is quite right," said the old mistress. "Let her go, Little Ingmar! You may as well know that otherwise I'll be the one to leave. I'll not sleep one night under the same roof with the likes of her."
"For God's sake, let me go!" Brita moaned.
Ingmar swore, turned the horse, and sprang into the cart. He was sick and tired of all this and could not stand any more of it.
Out on the highway they kept meeting churchgoers. This annoyed Ingmar. Suddenly he turned the horse and drove onto a narrow forest road.
As he turned, someone called to him. He glanced back. It was the postman with a letter for him. He took the letter, thrust it into his pocket, and drove on.
As soon as he felt sure he could not be seen from the road, he slowed down and brought out the letter. Instantly Brita put her hand on his arm. "Don't read it!" she begged.
"Why not?" he asked.
"Never mind reading it; it's nothing."
"But how can you know?"
"It's a letter from me."
"Then tell me yourself what's in it."
"No, I can't tell you that."
He looked hard at her. She turned scarlet, her eyes growing wild with alarm. "I think I will read that letter anyway," said Ingmar, and began to tear open the envelope.
"O Heavenly Father!" she cried. "Am I to be spared nothing? Ingmar," she implored, "read it in a day or two—when I am on my way to America."

By that time he had already opened the letter and was scanning it. She put her hand over the paper. "Listen to me, Ingmar!" she said. "It was the chaplain who got me to write that letter. He promised not to send it till I was on board the steamer. Instead he sent it off too soon. You have no right to read it yet. Wait till I'm gone, Ingmar."
Ingmar gave her an angry look and jumped out of the wagon so he could read the letter in peace. Brita was as agitated now as she had been in the old days, when things did not go her way.
"What I say in that letter isn't true. The chaplain talked me into writing it. I don't love you, Ingmar."

He looked up from the paper and gazed at her in astonishment. Then she grew silent, and the lessons in humility she had learned in prison served her now. After all, she suffered no greater embarrassment than she deserved.
Ingmar stood puzzling over the letter. Suddenly, with an impatient snarl, he crumpled it up.
"I can't make this out!" he said, stamping his foot. "My head's all in a muddle."
He went up to Brita and gripped her by the arm.
"Does it really say in the letter that you care for me?" His tone was shockingly brutal, and the look of him was terrible.
Brita was silent.
"Does the letter say that you care for me?" he repeated savagely.
"Yes," she answered faintly.
Then his face became horribly distorted. He shook her arm and thrust it from him. "How you can lie!" he said with a hoarse and angry laugh. "How you can lie!"
"God knows I have prayed night and day that I might see you again before I go!" she solemnly vowed.
"Where are you going?"
"I'm going to America, of course."
"The hell you are!"
Ingmar was beside himself. He staggered a few steps into the woods and cast himself upon the ground. And now it was his turn to weep!
Brita followed him and sat down beside him. She was so happy she wanted to shout.
"Ingmar, Little Ingmar!" she said, calling him by his pet name.
"But you think I'm so ugly!" he returned.
"Of course I do."
Ingmar pushed her hand away.
"Now let me tell you something," said Brita.
"Tell away."
"Do you remember what you said in court three years ago?"
"I do."
"That if I could only get to think differently of you, you would marry me?"
"Yes, I remember."

"It was after that I began to care for you. I had never imagined any mortal could say such a thing. It seemed almost unbelievable—your saying it to me, after all I had done to you. As I looked at you that day, I thought you better looking than all the others. You were wiser than any of them, and the only one with whom it would be good to share a life. I fell so deeply in love with you that it seemed as if you belonged to me and I to you. At first I took it for granted that you would come and fetch me, but later I hardly dared think it."
Ingmar raised his head. "Then why didn't you write?" he asked.
"But I did write."
"Asking me to forgive you, as if that were anything to write about!"
"What should I have written?"
"About the other thing."
"How would I have dared—I?"
"I came mighty near not coming at all."

"But Ingmar! Do you suppose I could have written love letters to you after all I had done! My last day in prison I wrote to you because the chaplain said I must. When I gave him the letter, he promised not to send it until I was well on my way."
Ingmar took her hand, flattened it against the earth, then slapped it.
"I could beat you!" he said.
"You may do with me what you will, Ingmar."
He looked up into her face, upon which suffering had worked a new kind of beauty. "And I came so near letting you go!" he sighed.
"You just had to come, I suppose."
"Let me tell you that I didn't care for you."
"I don't wonder at that."
"I felt relieved when I heard you were to be sent to America."
"Yes, father wrote me that you were pleased."
"Whenever I looked at mother, I felt somehow that I couldn't ask her to accept a daughter-in-law like you."
"No, it would never do, Ingmar."
"I've had to put up with a lot on your account. No one would notice me because of my treatment of you."
"Now you are doing what you threatened to do," said Brita. "You're striking me."
"I can't begin to tell you how furious I am at you."
She kept still.
"When I think of all I've had to stand these last few weeks—" he went on.
"But Ingmar—"
"Oh, I'm not angry about that, but at the thought of how near I came to letting you go!"
"Didn't you love me, Ingmar?"
"No, indeed."
"Not during the whole journey home?"
"No, not for a second! I was just put out with you."
"When did you change?"
"When I got your letter."
"I saw that your love was over. That was why I did not want you to know that mine was only just beginning."
Ingmar chuckled.
"What amuses you, Ingmar?"
"I'm thinking of how we sneaked out of church, and of the kind of welcome we got at the Ingmar Farm."
"And you can laugh at that?"
"Why not laugh? I suppose we'll have to take to the road, like tramps. Wonder what father would say to that?"
"You may laugh, Ingmar, but this can't be. It can't be."
"I think it can, for now I don't care a damn about anything or anybody but you!"

Brita was ready to cry, but he just made her tell him again and again how often she had thought of him and how much she had longed for him. Little by little he became as quiet as a child listening to a lullaby. It was all so different from what Brita had expected. She had thought of talking to him about her crime, if he came for her, and the weight of it. She would have liked to tell him or her mother, or whoever had come, how unworthy she was of them. But she had not been allowed to speak a word of this.
Presently he said very gently:
"There is something you want to tell me?"
"Yes."
"And you are thinking about it all the time?"
"Day and night!"
"And it gets sort of mixed in with everything?"
"That's true."
"Now tell me about it, so there will be two instead of one to bear it."
He sat looking into her eyes. They were like the eyes of a poor, hunted fawn. But as she spoke, they became calmer.
"Now you feel better," he said when she had finished.
"I feel as if a great weight has been lifted from my heart."
"That is because we are two to bear it. Now, perhaps, you won't want to go away."
"Indeed I should love to stay!" she said.
"Then let us go home," said Ingmar, rising.
"No, I'm afraid!"
"Mother is not so terrible," he laughed, "when she sees that someone has a mind of their own."
"No, Ingmar, I could never turn her out of her home. I have no choice but to go to America."
"I'm going to tell you something," said Ingmar with a mysterious smile. "You needn't be the least bit afraid, for there is someone who will help us."
"Who is it?"
"It's father. He'll see to it that everything comes out right."
Someone was coming along the forest road. It was Kaisa. But as she was not carrying her familiar yoke with the baskets, they hardly knew her at first.
"Good day to you!" Ingmar and Brita greeted her, and the old woman came up and shook hands with them.

"Well, I declare, here you sit, and all the folks from the farm are out looking for you! You were in such a hurry to get out of church," the old woman went on, "that I never got to meet you at all. So I went down to the farm to pay my respects to Brita. When I got there, who should I see but the Dean. He was in the house calling Mother Martha at the top of his lungs before I even had a chance to say how do you do. And before he had so much as shaken hands with her, he was crying out: 'Now, Mother Martha, you can be proud of Ingmar! It's plain now that he belongs to the old stock, so we must begin to call him Big Ingmar.'"

"Mother Martha, as you know, never says very much. She just stood there tying knots in her shawl. 'What's this you're telling me?' she said finally. 'He has brought Brita home,' the Dean explained. 'Believe me, Mother Martha, he will be honored and respected for it as long as he lives.' 'You don't tell me,' said the old lady. 'I could hardly go on with the service when I saw them sitting in church. It was a better sermon than any I could ever preach. Ingmar will be a credit to us all, as his father before him was.' 'The Dean brings us great news,' said Mother Martha. 'Isn't he home yet?' asked the Dean. 'No, he is not at home, but they may have stopped at Bergskog first.'"
"Did mother really say that?" cried Ingmar.
"Why, of course she did! And while we sat waiting for you to appear, she sent out one messenger after another to look for you."

Kaisa kept up a steady stream of talk, but Ingmar no longer heard what she said. His thoughts were far away. "I come into the living room, where father sits with all the old Ingmars. 'Good day to you, Big Ingmar Ingmarsson,' says father, rising and coming toward me. 'The same to you, father,' says I, 'and thank you for your help.' 'Now you'll be well married,' says father, 'and then the other matters will all right themselves.' 'But father, it could never have turned out so well if you hadn't stood by me.' 'That was nothing,' says father. 'All we Ingmars need do is to walk in the ways of God.'"

chapters.title: Book Two — At The Schoolmaster's
paragraphs: In the early 1880s, no one in the parish where the old Ingmarsson family lived would have thought of embracing any new kind of faith or attending any new form of worship. It was known that new sects had sprung up here and there in other Dalecarlian parishes, and that people went out into rivers and lakes to be immersed according to the new Baptist rites. But folks only laughed at it all and said: "That sort of thing may suit those who live at Applebo and in Gagnef, but it can never touch our parish."

The people of that parish clung to their old customs and habits. One of these was regular attendance at church on Sundays. Everyone who could go went, even in the most severe winter weather. Then, of all times, it was almost a necessity. With the thermometer at twenty below zero outside, it would have been beyond endurance to sit in the unheated church had it not been packed to the doors with people.

It could not be said that the parishioners turned out in such numbers because they had a particularly brilliant pastor or one with any special gift for preaching. In those days people went to church to praise God, not to be entertained by fine sermons. On the way home, fighting against the cutting wind on an open country road, you thought: "Our Lord must have noticed that I was at church this cold morning." That was the main thing. It was not the congregation's fault if the preacher had said nothing more than he had been heard to say every Sunday since his appointment.

In fact, the majority seemed perfectly satisfied with what they got. They knew that what the pastor read to them was the Word of God, and therefore they found it altogether beautiful. Only the schoolmaster and one or two of the more thoughtful farmers occasionally said among themselves: "The parson seems to have only one sermon. He talks of nothing but God's wisdom and God's government. All that is well enough so long as the Dissenters keep away. But this stronghold is poorly defended and would fall at the first attack."

Lay preachers generally passed this parish by. "What's the good of going there?" they used to say. "Those people don't want to be awakened." Not only the lay preachers but even all the "awakened souls" in neighboring parishes looked upon the Ingmarssons and their fellow parishioners as great sinners. Whenever they caught the sound of the bells from their church, they would say the bells were tolling, "Sleep in your sins! Sleep in your sins!"

The whole congregation, old and young, were furious when they learned that people spoke that way of their bells. They knew their folk never forgot to repeat the Lord's Prayer whenever the church bells rang. Every evening, at the time of the Angelus, the men uncovered their heads, the women curtsied, and everyone stood still about as long as it takes to say an Our Father. All who have lived in that parish must admit that God never seemed so mighty and so honored as on summer evenings, when scythes were rested and plows stopped in the middle of a furrow and the seed wagon halted in the midst of loading—simply at the stroke of a bell. It was as if they knew that our Lord at that moment was hovering over the parish on an evening cloud—great and powerful and good—breathing His blessing upon the whole community.

No college-educated man had ever taught in that parish. The schoolmaster was just a plain, old-fashioned farmer who was self-taught. He was a capable man who could manage a hundred children single-handed. For thirty years and more he had been the only teacher there, and everyone looked up to him. The schoolmaster seemed to feel that the spiritual welfare of the entire congregation rested with him. He was therefore quite concerned that they had called a parson who was no kind of preacher. However, he held his peace as long as it was only a question of introducing a new form of baptism elsewhere. But when he learned that there had also been changes in the Holy Communion and that people were gathering in private homes to partake of the Sacrament, he could no longer remain passive. Although a poor man himself, he persuaded some of the leading citizens to raise money for a mission house. "You know me," he said to them. "I only want to preach in order to strengthen people in the old faith. What would happen if the lay preachers came upon us with their new baptism and their new Sacrament, and there were no one to tell the people what was true doctrine and what was false?"

The schoolmaster was as well liked by the clergyman as by everyone else. He and the parson were frequently seen strolling together along the road between the schoolhouse and the parsonage, back and forth, back and forth, as if they had no end of things to say to each other. The parson would often drop in at the schoolmaster's of an evening to sit in the cozy kitchen by an open fire and chat with the schoolmaster's wife, Mother Stina. At times he came night after night. He had a dreary time of it at home—his wife was always ailing, and there was neither order nor comfort in his house.

One winter evening the schoolmaster and his wife were sitting by the kitchen fire, talking in earnest whispers, while a little girl of twelve played by herself in a corner of the room. The little girl was their daughter, and her name was Gertrude. She was a fair little thing with flaxen hair and plump rosy cheeks, but she did not have that wise and prematurely old look you so often see in the children of schoolmasters.

The corner where she sat was her playground. She had gathered together a variety of things there: bits of colored glass, broken teacups and saucers, pebbles from the riverbank, little square blocks of wood, and more odds and ends of the same sort.

She had been left to play in peace all evening. Neither her father nor her mother had disturbed her. Busy as she was, she did not want to be reminded of lessons and chores. It didn't look as if there were going to be any extra sums to do for father that night, she thought.

She had a big project in hand, the little girl back there in her corner. Nothing less than making a whole parish! She was going to build up the entire district with both church and schoolhouse. The river and the bridge were also to be included. Everything had to be quite complete, of course.

She had already gotten a good part of it done. The whole ring of hills that went round the parish was made up of smaller and larger stones. In all the crevices she had planted forests of little spruce twigs, and with two jagged stones she had erected Klack Mountain and Olaf's Peak on either side of the Dal River. The long valley between the mountains had been covered with soil taken from one of her mother's flowerpots. So far everything was all right. She just hadn't been able to make the valley bloom. But she comforted herself by pretending it was early springtime, before grass and grain had sprouted.

The broad, beautiful Dal River that flows through the valley she had laid out with a long, narrow piece of glass. The floating bridge connecting both sides of the parish had been sitting on the water for some time. The more distant farms and settlements were marked off by pieces of red brick. Farthest north, amid fields and meadows, lay the Ingmar Farm. To the east was the village of Kolasen, at the foot of the mountain. At the extreme south, where the river with its rapids and falls leaves the valley and rushes under the mountain, was Bergsana Foundry.

The entire landscape was now ready, with country roads laid out along the river, sanded and graveled. Groves had been set out here and there on the plains and near the cottages. The little girl had only to glance at her structure of glass and stone and earth and twigs to see the whole parish before her. And she thought it all very beautiful.

Time after time she raised her head to call her mother and show her what she had done, then changed her mind. She had always found it wiser not to call attention to herself. But the most difficult work was yet to come: building the town on both sides of the river. It meant much shifting about of stones and bits of glass. The sheriff's house wanted to crowd out the merchant's shop. There was no room for the judge's house next to the doctor's. There were the church and the parsonage, the drugstore and post office, the peasant homesteads with their barns and outhouses, the inn, the hunter's lodge, the telegraph station. To remember everything was no small task!

Finally the whole town of white and red houses stood embedded in green. Now there was only one thing left. She had worked hard to get everything else done so she could begin on the schoolhouse. She wanted plenty of space for the school, which was to be built on the riverside, and must have a big yard with a flagpole right in the middle of the lawn.

She had saved all her best blocks for the schoolhouse. Now she wondered how best to go about it. She wanted it to be just like their school, with a big classroom on the ground floor and another upstairs. Then there was the kitchen and also the big room where she and her parents lived. But all that would take a good while. "They won't leave me in peace long enough," she said to herself.

Just then footsteps were heard in the entry. Someone was stamping off snow. In a flash she went on with her building. "Here comes the parson to chat with father and mother," she thought. Now she would have the whole evening to herself. With renewed courage she began to lay the foundation of a schoolhouse as big as half the parish.
Her mother, who had also heard the steps in the hall, got up quickly and drew an old armchair up to the fireplace. Then, turning to her husband, she said: "Shall you tell him about it tonight?"
"Yes," answered the schoolmaster, "as soon as I can get around to it."

Presently the pastor came in, half frozen and glad to be in a warm room where he could sit by an open fire. He was very talkative, as usual. It would be hard to find a more likable man than the parson when he came in of an evening to chat about all sorts of things, big and little. He spoke with such ease and assurance about everything pertaining to this world that you could scarcely believe he and the dull preacher were one and the same person. But if you happened to speak to him about spiritual matters, you got nothing out of him. He would turn things over and look at them from this side and that without ever arriving at a conclusion.
When the parson had settled himself comfortably, the schoolmaster suddenly turned to him and said in a cheerful tone:
"Now I must tell you the news: I'm going to build a mission house."
The clergyman became white as a sheet and sank back in his chair.
"What are you saying, Storm?" he gasped. "Are they really thinking of building a mission house here? Then what's to become of me and the church? Are we to be dispensed with?"

"The church and the pastor will be needed just the same," the schoolmaster returned with confidence. "It is my purpose that the mission house shall promote the welfare of the church. With so many sects cropping up all over the country, the church is sorely in need of help."

"I thought you were my friend, Storm," said the parson mournfully. Only a few moments before he had come in confident and happy. Now all at once his spirit was gone, and he looked as if he were entirely done for.

The schoolmaster understood quite well why the pastor was so distressed. He and everyone else knew that the clergyman had once been a man of rare promise. But in his student days he had gone too far, so to speak, and suffered a stroke as a result. After that he was never the same. Sometimes he seemed to forget that he was only the ruin of a man. But when reminded of it, a sense of deep despondency came over him. Now he sat there as if paralyzed. It was a long time before anyone spoke.
"You mustn't take it like that, Parson," the schoolmaster said at last, trying to make his voice very soft and low.
"Hush, Storm! I know I'm not a great preacher. Still, I couldn't have believed it possible that you would wish to take the living from me."
Storm made a gesture of protest, which said in effect that anything of the sort had never entered his mind. But he had not the courage to put it into words.

The schoolmaster was a man of sixty and, despite all the work and responsibility that had fallen to his lot, was still master of his faculties. There was a great contrast between him and the parson. Storm was one of the biggest men in Dalecarlia. His head was covered with a mass of black bushy hair, his skin was dark as bronze, and his features were strong and clear-cut. He looked singularly powerful beside the pastor, who was a little narrow-chested, bald-headed man.

The schoolmaster's wife thought that her husband, as the stronger, ought to give in, and motioned him to drop the matter. Whatever regret he may have felt, there was nothing in his manner to suggest he had any idea of abandoning his project.

Then the schoolmaster began to speak plainly and to the point. He said he was certain that before long the heretics would invade their parish. Therefore it was very necessary to have a meeting place where one could talk to the people in a more informal way than at a regular church service. A place where one might choose one's own text, expound the whole Bible, and interpret its most difficult passages.

His wife again signed to him to keep still. She knew what the clergyman was thinking while her husband talked. "So I haven't taught them anything, and I haven't given them any protection against unbelief? I must be a poor specimen of a pastor when the schoolmaster in my own parish thinks himself a better preacher than I."
The schoolmaster, however, did not keep still. He went on talking of all that must be done to protect the flock from the wolves.
"I haven't seen any wolves," said the pastor.
"But I know they are on their way."
"And you, Storm, are opening the door to them," declared the minister, rising. The schoolmaster's talk had irritated him. The blood mounted to his face, and he regained a little of his old dignity.

"My dear Storm, let us drop the subject," he said. Then, turning to the housewife, he made some pleasant remark about the last pretty bride she had dressed. For Mother Stina dressed all the brides in the parish.

Peasant woman though she was, she understood how it must hurt him to be so cruelly reminded of his own weakness. She wept from compassion and could not answer him for the tears. So the pastor had to do most of the talking.

Meanwhile he kept thinking: "Oh, if I only had some of the power and capacity of my younger days, I would convince this peasant at once of the wrong he is doing." With that he turned again to the schoolmaster:
"Where did you get the money, Storm?" he asked.

"A company has been formed," Storm explained. Then he mentioned the names of several men who had pledged their support, just to show the parson that they were the kind of people who would harm neither the church nor its pastor.
"Is Ingmar Ingmarsson in it, too?" the parson exclaimed. The effect was like a deathblow. "And to think that I was as sure of Ingmar Ingmarsson as I had been of you, Storm!"

He said nothing more about this just then, but instead turned to Mother Stina and talked to her. He must have seen that she was crying, but acted as if he had not noticed. After a little while he addressed the schoolmaster again.
"Drop it, Storm!" he begged. "Drop it for my sake. You wouldn't like it if somebody put up another school next to yours."
The schoolmaster sat gazing at the floor and reflected a moment. Presently he said, almost reluctantly, "I can't, Parson."
For a full ten minutes there was a dead silence. Then the pastor put on his overcoat and cap and went toward the door.

The whole evening he had been trying to find words to prove to Storm that he was not only doing harm to the pastor with this undertaking, but undermining the parish itself. Although thoughts and words kept crowding into his head, he could neither arrange them into an orderly sequence nor give them voice, because he was a broken man. Walking toward the door, he spotted Gertrude sitting in her corner, playing with her blocks and bits of glass. He stopped and looked at her. Evidently she had been working very hard. Her round cheeks were flushed, her eyes sparkled, and her little face was beaming with happiness. Her creations, her buildings, and her roadways, which she had fashioned from nothing, completely absorbed her.
The pastor was startled by the sight of all this innocent happiness in contrast to his own heavy heart.
"What are you making?" he asked, and went up to her.
The little girl had finished her parish long before. In fact, she had already pulled it down and started something new.
"If you had only come a minute sooner!" the child exclaimed. "I had made such a beautiful parish, with both church and schoolhouse—"
"But where is it now?"
"Oh, I've destroyed the parish, and now I'm building a Jerusalem, and—"
"What?" the parson interrupted. "Have you destroyed the parish in order to build a Jerusalem?"
"Yes," said Gertrude, "and it was such a fine parish! But we read about Jerusalem yesterday in school, and now I have pulled down the parish to build a Jerusalem."
The preacher stood looking at the child. He put his hand to his forehead and thought a moment, then said: "It is surely someone greater than you that speaks through your mouth."

The child's words seemed so extraordinarily prophetic that he kept repeating them to himself, over and over. Gradually his thoughts drifted back into their old groove, and he began to ponder the ways of Providence and the means by which He works His will.
Presently he went back to the schoolmaster, his eyes shining with a new light, and said in his usual cheerful tone:

"I'm no longer angry at you, Storm. You are only doing what you must do. All my life I have been pondering the ways of Providence, and I can't seem to get any light on them. Nor do I understand this thing, but I understand that you are doing what you must."

chapters.title: Book Two — And They Saw Heaven Open
paragraphs: The spring the mission house was built, there was a great thaw, and the Dal River rose to an alarming height. What quantities of water that spring brought! It came in showers from the sky. It came rushing down in streams from the mountainsides. It welled out of the earth. Water ran in every wheel rut and every furrow. All this water found its way to the river, which kept rising higher and higher, rolling onward with greater and greater force. It no longer had its usual shiny and merry appearance. Now it was gray and dirty. It was choked with logs and ice floes and branches and bundles of straw, and looked as fierce and menacing as a beast that has broken from its cage.
At first the grown folks paid no special attention to the spring flood. Only the children ran down to the banks to watch the raging river and all that it carried along.
But timber and ice floes were not the only things floating by! Soon the stream came driving with washing piers and bathhouses, then with boats and wreckage of bridges.
"It will soon be taking our bridge, too!" the children exclaimed. They felt a bit uneasy but were glad at the same time that something so extraordinary was likely to happen.

Suddenly a huge pine, root and branch, came sailing past, followed by a white-stemmed aspen tree with spreading branches thick with buds that had swelled from being so long in the water. Close behind the trees came a little hay shed, bottom upward. It was still full of hay and straw and floated on its roof like a boat on its keel.

But when things of that sort began to drift past, the grown-ups also bestirred themselves. They realized now that the river had overflowed its banks somewhere up north. They hurried down to the shores with poles and boat hooks to haul buildings and furniture up on land.

At the northern end of the parish, where the houses were scattered and people were scarce, Ingmar Ingmarsson stood alone on the bank, gazing out at the river. He was then almost sixty and looked even older. His face was weatherbeaten and furrowed, his figure bent. He appeared to be as awkward and helpless as ever. He stood leaning on a long, heavy boat hook, his dull, sleepy-looking eyes fixed on the water. The river raged and foamed, arrogantly marching past with all it had snatched from the lands above. Here and there you could see the floor of a house with some article of furniture still fastened to it. A chair or table would stand upright on the floor as it floated along, as if placed there by some unseen hand.

Ingmar Ingmarsson made no attempt to rescue any of the floating bridges or boat hulls that passed quite close to the bank. "All that will be seen to down at the village," he thought. Not for a second did his gaze wander from the river. He took note of everything that drifted past. All at once he spotted something bright and yellow floating on some loosely nailed boards quite a distance upriver. "Ah, this is what I have been expecting all along!" he said aloud. At first he could not quite make out what it was, but it looked as if some of those yellow birch-bark baskets in which children are rocked to sleep had been set on the boards.

It was not long before the peasant saw that he had guessed rightly. Now he could clearly see three little children in their yellow homespun frocks and round yellow hats, being carried downstream on a poorly built raft that was slowly being torn apart by the swift current and the moving ice floes.

The children were still a long way off. Big Ingmar knew there was a bend in the river where it touched his land. If God in His mercy would only direct the raft into this current, he thought, he might be able to get them ashore.

He stood very still, watching the raft. All at once it seemed as if someone had given it a push. It swung round and headed straight for the shore. By that time the children were so close he could see their frightened little faces and hear their cries. But they were still too far out to be reached by the boat hook from the bank. So he hurried down to the water's edge and waded into the river.
As he did so, he had a strange feeling that someone was calling him to come back. "You are no longer a young man, Ingmar. This may prove a dangerous business for you!" a voice said to him.

He thought a moment, wondering whether he had the right to risk his life. The wife whom he had once fetched from prison had died during the winter, and since her death his one longing had been that he might soon follow. But on the other hand, there was his son who needed a father's care, for he was only a little lad and could not look after the farm.
"In any case, it must be as God wills," he said.

Now Big Ingmar was no longer either awkward or slow. As he plunged into the raging river, he planted his boat hook firmly in the bottom so as not to be carried away by the current. He took good care to dodge the floating ice and driftwood. When the raft with the children was quite near, he pressed his feet down into the riverbed, thrust out his boat hook, and got a grip on it.

"Hold on tight!" he shouted to the children, for just then the raft made a sudden turn and all its planks creaked. But the wretched structure held together, and Big Ingmar managed to pull it out of the strongest current. That done, he let go of it, for he knew the raft would now drift shoreward by itself.

Touching bottom with his boat hook again, he turned to go back to the bank. This time, however, he failed to notice a huge log rushing toward him. It caught him in the side just below the armpit. It was a terrific blow, for the log was hurled against him with a force that sent him staggering in the water. Yet he kept a tight grip on the boat hook until he reached the bank. When he again stood on firm ground, he hardly dared touch his body, for he felt that his chest had been crushed. "I have received my death blow," he said calmly, and walked slowly home.

The pastor was called in and remained at the Ingmar Farm the whole afternoon. On his way home, he stopped at the schoolmaster's. He had experienced things in the course of the day that he felt the need of telling to someone who would understand.

Storm and Mother Stina were deeply grieved, for they had already heard that Ingmar Ingmarsson was dead. The clergyman, on the other hand, looked almost radiant as he stepped into the schoolmaster's kitchen.
Storm immediately asked the pastor if he had been in time.
"Yes," he said, "but on this occasion I was not needed."
"Weren't you?" said Mother Stina.
