"No," answered the pastor with a mysterious smile. "He would have gotten on just as well without me. Sometimes it is very hard to sit by a deathbed," he added.
"It is indeed," nodded the schoolmaster.
"Particularly when the one who is passing from among us happens to be the best man in your parish."
"Just so."
"But things can also be quite different from what one had imagined."
For a moment the pastor sat quietly gazing into space. His eyes looked clearer than usual behind the spectacles.
"Have you, Storm, or you, Mother Stina, ever heard of the wonderful thing that once happened to Big Ingmar when he was a young man?" he asked.
The schoolmaster said he had heard many wonderful things about him.

"Why, of course. But this is the most wonderful of all! I never knew of it myself until today. Big Ingmar had a good friend who has always lived in a little cabin on his estate," the pastor continued.
"Yes, I know," said the schoolmaster. "He is also named Ingmar. Folks call him Strong Ingmar, to tell them apart."

"True," said the pastor. "His father named him Ingmar in honor of the master's family. One Saturday evening at midsummer, when the nights are almost as light as the days, Big Ingmar and his friend Strong Ingmar finished their work, put on their Sunday clothes, and went down to the village looking for amusement."

The pastor paused a moment and pondered. "I can imagine the night must have been a beautiful one," he went on. "Clear and still—one of those nights when earth and sky seem to exchange hues, the sky turning a bright green while the earth becomes veiled in white mists, lending everything a white or bluish tinge. When Big Ingmar and Strong Ingmar were crossing the bridge to the village, it was as if someone told them to stop and look upward. They did so. And they saw heaven open! They saw a brilliant light and angels swinging their censers, and they could hear music as beautiful as the ringing of silver bells."

The pastor closed his eyes for a moment and heaved a deep sigh. "I have never before heard of such things." His voice shook a little as he continued. "I only wish I had stood on the bridge with Big Ingmar and Strong Ingmar and seen heaven open!"

"This morning, immediately after Big Ingmar had been carried home, he asked that Strong Ingmar be sent for. A messenger was dispatched to the croft at once to fetch him, only to find that Strong Ingmar was not at home. He was in the forest somewhere, chopping firewood, and was not easy to find. Messenger after messenger went in search of him. In the meantime, Big Ingmar felt very anxious, fearing he might not get to see his old friend again in this life. First the doctor came, then I came, but still no Strong Ingmar. Big Ingmar suffered greatly and took no notice of the rest of us. Only the children could comfort him. Whenever the pain became too much, he would call the children to him. He has two—a boy named Ingmar, who is about four, and a girl named Brita, who is about six. He would take the little ones in his arms and hold them fast, and whenever he felt a sharp pang he would press them to his heart. But the moment it passed, he let them go."

"At last they found the crofter. Big Ingmar glanced away from the children with a sigh of relief when he heard Strong Ingmar's heavy step in the hallway. When his friend came over to the bedside, he took his hand and patted it gently, saying: 'Do you remember the time when you and I stood on the bridge and saw heaven open?' 'As if I could ever forget that night when we two had a vision of Paradise!' Strong Ingmar responded. Then Big Ingmar turned toward him, his face beaming with joy, and said: 'Today you and I shall go on a pilgrimage together.' Those were his last words. A moment later he was dead."
The schoolmaster and his wife thought, with the pastor, that it was a beautiful death. All three of them sat profoundly silent for a long while.
"But what could Strong Ingmar have meant," asked Mother Stina suddenly, "when he spoke of the pilgrimage?"

The pastor looked up, somewhat perplexed. "I don't know," he replied. "Big Ingmar died just after that was said, and I have not had time to ponder it." He fell to thinking, then spoke half to himself: "It was a strange sort of thing to say. You're right about that, Mother Stina."
"You know, of course, that it has been said of Strong Ingmar that he can see into the future?" she said thoughtfully.

The pastor sat stroking his forehead in an effort to collect his thoughts. "The ways of Providence cannot be reasoned out by the finite mind," he mused. "I cannot fathom them. Yet seeking to know them is the most satisfying thing in all the world."

chapters.title: Book Two — Karin, Daughter Of Ingmar
paragraphs: Autumn had come and school was open again. One morning, when the children were having their recess, the schoolmaster and Gertrude went into the kitchen and sat down at the table, where Mother Stina served them coffee. Before they had finished their cups, a visitor arrived.

The caller was a young peasant named Halvor Halvorsson, who had lately opened a shop in the village. He came from Tims Farm and was known as Tims Halvor. He was a tall, good-looking fellow who appeared somewhat dejected. Mother Stina asked him to have some coffee too, so he sat down at the table, helped himself, and began to talk to the schoolmaster.

Mother Stina sat by the window knitting. From where she was seated she could look down the road. All at once she grew red in the face and leaned forward to get a better view. Trying to appear unconcerned, she said with feigned indifference: "The grand folk seem to be out walking today."
Tims Halvor thought he detected something peculiar in her tone. He got up and looked out. He saw a tall, stoop-shouldered woman and a half-grown boy coming toward the schoolhouse.
"Unless my eyes deceive me, that's Karin, daughter of Ingmar!" said Mother Stina.

"It's Karin all right," Tims Halvor confirmed. He said nothing more but turned away from the window and glanced around the room, as if trying to discover some way of escape. But in a moment he quietly went back to his seat.

The summer before, when Big Ingmar was still alive, Halvor had courted Karin Ingmarsson. The courtship had been a long one, with many ifs and buts on the part of her family. The old Ingmars were not quite sure he was good enough for Karin. It had not been a question of money, for Halvor was well-to-do. His father, however, had been addicted to drink, and who could say but that this failing had been passed on to the son. In the end, it was decided that Halvor should have Karin. But when Big Ingmar died in the spring, the engagement was broken off. Karin said to Halvor: "Now father is dead, and I cannot leave the farm in the care of the younger children." Halvor had to accept this. Though he felt badly treated, he could hardly argue with her in the midst of her grief. Besides, he quite understood that she was needed at home. She had six younger sisters who were still unprovided for, and a little brother who was only four years old.

Halvor took it very much to heart. "You are heaping shame upon me that will be hard to bear," he said. "What will people think if you throw me over like this? It isn't fair to treat a decent man that way."

But Karin would not be moved. Ever since, Halvor had been morose and unhappy. He could not forget the injustice the Ingmarssons had done him. And here sat Halvor, and there came Karin! What would happen next? This much was certain: a reconciliation was out of the question. Since the previous autumn Karin had been married to one Elof Ersson. She and her husband lived at the Ingmar Farm, which they had been running since the death of Big Ingmar in the spring. Big Ingmar had left no will, but Karin considered it her duty to hold the property together until her brother came of age.

Meanwhile Karin had come in. She was only about twenty-two but was one of those women who never look truly young. Most people thought her exceedingly plain, for she favored her father's family and had their heavy eyelids, their sandy hair, and hard lines about the mouth. But the schoolmaster and his wife were pleased to think she bore such a striking resemblance to the old Ingmars. When Karin saw Halvor, her face did not change. She moved about slowly and quietly, greeting each of them in turn.
"So Karin has really ventured out today?" said Mother Stina, drawing up the pastor's chair for her.
"Yes," she answered. "It's easy walking now that the frost has set in."
"There has been a hard frost during the night," the schoolmaster put in.
This was followed by a dead silence that lasted several minutes. Presently Halvor got up, and the others started, as if suddenly wakened from a sound sleep.
"I must get back to the shop," said Halvor.
"What's your hurry?" asked Mother Stina.
"I hope Halvor isn't going on my account," said Karin meekly.

As soon as Halvor was gone the tension was broken, and the schoolmaster knew at once what to say. He looked at the lad Karin had brought with her, whom no one had taken any notice of before. He was a little fellow who could not have been much older than Gertrude. He had a fair, soft baby face, yet there was something about him that made him appear old for his years. It was easy to tell which family he belonged to.
"I think Karin has brought us a new pupil," said Storm.
"This is my brother," Karin replied. "He is the present Ingmar Ingmarsson."
"He's rather little for that name," Storm remarked.
"Yes, father died too soon!"
"He did indeed," said the schoolmaster and his wife, both in the same breath.
"He has been attending the school in Falun," Karin explained. "That's why he hasn't been here before."
"Aren't you going to let him go back this year too?"
Karin dropped her eyes and a sigh escaped her. "He has the name of being a good student," she said, evading his question.
"I'm only afraid I can't teach him anything. He must know as much as I do."

"Well, I expect the schoolmaster knows a good deal more than a little fellow like him." Then came another pause, after which Karin continued: "This is not only about his attending school. I would also like to ask whether you and Mother Stina would let the boy come here to live."
The schoolmaster and his wife looked at each other in astonishment, but neither was prepared to answer.
"I'm afraid our quarters are rather tight," said Storm presently.
"I thought perhaps you might be willing to accept milk and butter and eggs as part of the payment."
"As to that—"
"You would be doing me a great service," said the rich peasant woman.
Mother Stina felt that Karin would never have made this unusual request without good reason. So she promptly settled the matter.
"Karin need say no more. We will do all we can for the Ingmarssons."
"Thank you," said Karin.

The two women talked over what had best be done for Ingmar's welfare. Meanwhile Storm took the boy with him to the classroom and gave him a seat next to Gertrude. During the whole of the first day, Ingmar never said a word.

Tims Halvor did not go near the schoolhouse again for a week or more. It was as if he were afraid of meeting Karin there again. But one morning when it rained in torrents, and there was no chance of any customers coming, he decided to run over and have a chat with Mother Stina. He was hungry for a heart-to-heart talk with some kindly and sympathetic person. He had been seized by a terrible fit of the blues. "I'm no good, and no one has any respect for me," he kept telling himself, tormenting himself as unhappy people do.

He closed his shop, buttoned his storm coat, and made his way to the school through wind and rain and slush. Halvor was happy to be back in the friendly atmosphere of the schoolhouse. He was still there when the recess bell rang and Storm and the two children came in for their coffee. All three went over to greet him. He rose to shake hands with the schoolmaster, but when little Ingmar put out his hand, Halvor was talking so earnestly to Mother Stina that he seemed not to have noticed the boy.
"Halvor has come to show us his new watch," said Mother Stina.

Halvor took from his pocket a new silver watch, which he showed to them. It was a pretty little timepiece with a flower design engraved on the case. The schoolmaster opened it, went into the schoolroom for a magnifying glass, adjusted it to his eye, and began examining the works. He seemed quite carried away as he studied the delicate adjustment of the tiny wheels, and said he had never seen finer workmanship. Finally he gave the watch back to Halvor, who put it in his pocket, looking pleased but trying not to show it.
Ingmar was silent during the meal, but when he had finished his coffee, he asked Storm whether he really knew anything about watches.
"Why, of course," the schoolmaster returned. "Don't you know that I understand a little of everything?"

Ingmar then brought out a watch he carried in his vest pocket. It was a big, round, silver turnip that looked ugly and clumsy compared with Halvor's watch. The chain was also a clumsy thing. The case was quite plain and dented. It was not much of a watch—it had no crystal, and the enamel on its face was cracked.
"It has stopped," said Storm, putting the watch to his ear.
"Yes, I kn-n-ow," stammered the boy. "I was just wondering if you didn't think it could be mended."
Storm opened it and found that all the wheels were loose. "You must have been hammering nails with this watch," he said. "I can't do anything with it."
"Don't you think Eric the clockmaker could fix it?"
"No, no more than I. You'd better send it to Falun and have new works put in."
"I thought so," said Ingmar, and took the watch back.
"For heaven's sake, what have you been doing with it?" the schoolmaster exclaimed.
The boy swallowed hard. "It was father's watch," he explained, "and it got damaged like that when father was struck by the log."
Now they all grew interested.

With an effort to control his feelings, Ingmar continued: "As you know, it happened during Holy Week, when I was home. I was the first person to reach father when he lay on the bank. I found him with the watch in his hand. 'Now it's all over with me, Ingmar,' he said. 'I'm sorry the watch is broken, for I want you to give it, with my greetings, to someone that I have wronged.' Then he told me who was to have the watch, and asked me to take it to Falun and have it repaired before presenting it."
The schoolmaster was wondering whether he knew of anyone who was soon going to the city, when Mother Stina turned to the boy:
"Who was to have the watch, Ingmar?" she asked.
"I don't know if I ought to tell," the boy demurred.
"Wasn't it Tims Halvor, who is sitting here?"
"Yes," he whispered.
"Then give Halvor the watch just as it is," said Mother Stina. "That will please him best."
Ingmar obediently rose, took out the watch, and rubbed it on the sleeve of his coat to shine it up a bit. Then he went over to Halvor.
"Father asked me to give you this with his compliments," he said, holding out the watch.

All this while Halvor had sat there, silent and glum. When the boy went over to him, he put his hand up to his eyes, as if he did not want to look at him. Ingmar stood a long time holding out the watch. Finally he glanced appealingly at Mother Stina.
"Blessed are the peacemakers," she said.

Then Storm put in a word. "I don't think you could ask for a better amend, Halvor," he said. "I've always maintained that if Ingmar Ingmarsson had lived he would have given you full justice long before this."
The next thing they saw was Halvor reaching out for the watch, almost as if against his will. But the moment he had it in his hand, he put it in the inside pocket of his vest.
"There's no fear of anyone taking that watch from him," said the schoolmaster with a laugh, as he saw Halvor carefully buttoning his coat.
And Halvor laughed too. Presently he got up, straightened himself, and drew a deep breath. The color came into his cheeks, and his eyes shone with a newfound happiness.
"Now Halvor must feel like a new man," said the schoolmaster's wife.

Then Halvor put his hand inside his overcoat and drew out his brand-new watch. Crossing over to Ingmar, who was again seated at the table, he said: "Since I have taken your father's watch from you, you must accept this one from me."

He laid the watch on the table and went out, without even saying goodbye. The rest of the day he tramped the roads and bypaths. A couple of peasants who had come from a distance to trade with him hung around outside the shop from noon till evening. But no Tims Halvor appeared.

Elof Ersson, the husband of Karin Ingmarsson, was the son of a cruel and miserly peasant who had always treated him harshly. As a child he had been half starved, and even after he was grown up his father kept him under his thumb. He had to toil and slave from morning till night and was never allowed any pleasures. He was not even allowed to attend the country dances like other young folk, and he got no rest from his work even on Sundays. Nor did Elof become his own master when he married. He came to live at the Ingmar Farm, where Big Ingmar was the law. The old man was not strict, exactly, but he expected his will to be obeyed without any back talk.

But as soon as Big Ingmar was dead and buried, Elof began to drink and carouse. He made the acquaintance of every ne'er-do-well in the parish, invited them down to the Farm, and went with them to dance halls and taverns. He quit work altogether and drank himself full every day. In the space of two short months he became a poor drunken wreck.

The first time Karin saw him drunk, she was horrified. "This is God's judgment upon me for my treatment of Halvor," was her first thought. To her husband she said very little by way of rebuke or warning. She soon saw that he was like a blasted tree, doomed to wither and decay. She could not hope for either help or protection from him.

But Karin's sisters were not so wise. They resented his escapades, blushed at his crude songs and coarse jokes, by turns threatening and scolding him. Though their brother-in-law was on the whole rather good-natured, he sometimes flew into a rage and had words with them. Then Karin's only thought was how to get her sisters away from the house, so they might escape the misery in which she herself had to live. Over the course of the summer she managed to marry off the two eldest. In the fall she sent the four younger girls to schools in various towns.

All the sisters received their share of the inheritance, which amounted to twenty thousand kroner each. The farm had been left to Karin, with the understanding that young Ingmar was to take it over when he came of age.

It seemed remarkable that Karin, who was so awkward and shy, should have been able to send so many birds from the nest, find mates for them, and homes. She arranged it all herself, for she could get no help whatever from her husband, who had now become utterly worthless.

Her greatest concern, however, was the little brother—he who was now Ingmar Ingmarsson. The boy provoked Karin's husband even more than the sisters had. He did it by actions rather than words. Once he poured out all the corn brandy Elof had brought home. Another time the brother-in-law caught him in the act of diluting his liquor with water.
When autumn came, Karin insisted that the boy be sent back to school in Falun that year, as in the past. But her husband, who was also his guardian, would not hear of it.

"Ingmar shall be a farmer, like his father and me and my father," said Elof. "What business has he at school? When winter comes, he and I will go into the forest to put up charcoal kilns. That will be the best kind of schooling for him. When I was his age, I spent a whole winter working at the kiln."
As Karin could not make him change his mind, she had to accept it and keep Ingmar at home for the time being.

Elof then tried to win the boy's confidence. Whenever he went anywhere, he always wanted Ingmar to come along. The lad went, of course, but unwillingly. He did not like going with him on his sprees. Then Elof would coax the boy and swear he was not going any farther than the church or the shop. But once he got Ingmar in the cart, he would drive off with him down to the smithies at Bergsana or the tavern in Karmsund.
Karin was glad her husband took the boy along. It was at least a safeguard against Elof being left in a ditch by the roadside or driving the horse to death.
Once, when Elof came home at eight in the morning, Ingmar was sitting beside him in the cart, fast asleep.
"Come out here and look after the boy!" Elof shouted to Karin. "Carry him in. The poor brat's as drunk as a lord and can't walk a step."

Karin was so shocked she almost collapsed. She had to sit down on the steps for a moment to recover herself before she could lift the boy. The minute she took hold of him, she discovered that he was not really asleep but stiff from the cold and unconscious. Taking the boy in her arms, she carried him into the bedroom, locked the door behind her, and tried to bring him around. After a while she stepped into the living room, where Elof sat eating his breakfast. She walked straight up to him.
"You'd better eat a good meal while you're at it," she said, "for if you have made my brother drink himself to death, you'll soon have to put up with poorer fare than you get at the Ingmar Farm."
"How you talk! As if a little brandy could hurt him!"
"Mark what I say! If the boy dies, you'll get twenty years in prison, Elof."
When Karin returned to the bedroom, the boy had come out of his stupor but was delirious and unable to move hand or foot. He suffered agonies.
"Do you think I'm going to die, Karin?" he moaned.
"No, dear, of course not," Karin assured him.
"I didn't know what they were giving me."
"Thank God for that!" said Karin fervently.
"If I die, write to my sisters and tell them I didn't know it was liquor," the boy wailed.
"Yes, dear," Karin soothed.
"Really and truly I didn't know—I swear it!"
All day Ingmar lay in a raging fever. "Please don't tell father about it!" he raved.
"Father will never know of it," she said.
"But suppose I die. Then father would surely find out, and I would be shamed before him."
"But it wasn't your fault, child."

"Maybe father will think I shouldn't have taken what Elof offered me? Don't you suppose the whole parish must know I was drunk?" he asked. "What do the hired men say, and what does old Lisa say, and Strong Ingmar?"
"They're not saying anything," Karin replied.

"You will have to tell them how it happened. We were at the tavern in Karmsund, where Elof and some of his pals had been drinking all night. I was sitting in a corner on a bench, half asleep, when Elof came over and roused me. 'Wake up, Ingmar,' he said very pleasantly, 'and I'll give you something to make you warm. Drink this,' he urged, holding a glass to my lips. 'It's only hot water with a little sugar in it.' I was shivering with cold when I woke, and as I drank the stuff, it certainly made me warm. 'Give me some more,' I begged. 'Let the boy have all he wants,' said Elof to the others; 'he hasn't tasted anything like it before.'"
Then Karin opened the door to the living room, where Elof still lingered over his meal. She felt it would be well for him to hear this.
"If only father were living, Karin, if only father were living!"
"What then, Ingmar?"
"Don't you think he'd kill him?"
Elof broke into a loud laugh, and when the boy heard him, he turned so pale with fright that Karin promptly closed the door again.
It had this good effect on Elof, at any rate: he put up no objection when Karin decided to take the boy to Storm's school.

Soon after Halvor had received the watch, his shop was always full of people. Every farmer in the parish, when in town, would stop at Halvor's shop to hear the story of Big Ingmar's watch. The peasants in their long white fur coats stood leaning over the counter by the hour, their solemn, furrowed faces turned toward Halvor as he talked. Sometimes he would take out the watch and show them the dented case and the cracked face.
"So that's where the blow caught him," the peasants would say. They seemed to see before them what had happened when Big Ingmar was hurt. "It is a great thing for you, Halvor, to have that watch!"
When Halvor showed the watch he would never let it out of his hands, but always kept a tight grip on the chain.

One day Halvor stood talking to a group of peasants, telling them the usual story, and at the high point the watch was of course brought out. As it was being passed from one to another—he holding the chain—a solemn hush fell over everyone. Meanwhile Elof had come into the shop, but since everyone's attention was on the watch, no one noticed him. Elof had also heard the story of his father-in-law's watch, and knew at once what was going on. He did not begrudge Halvor the gift; in fact, he thought it a fine thing. But he was jealous, and it irked him that Big Ingmar's memory had come to be linked with Halvor rather than with himself.
Elof crept quietly up behind the men, reached over, and snatched the watch from Halvor. It was only meant in fun. He had no thought of actually taking the watch—he just wanted to tease him a bit.

When Halvor tried to snatch it back, Elof stepped away and held it up, as if he were holding out a lump of sugar to a dog. Then Halvor vaulted the counter. He looked so angry that Elof got frightened and, instead of standing still and handing back the watch, he ran for the door.
Outside were some badly worn wooden steps. Elof's foot caught in a hole, and down he went. Halvor fell upon him, seized the watch, then gave him several hard kicks.
"You'd better quit kicking me and find out what's wrong with my back," said Elof.
Halvor stopped at once, but Elof made no move to raise himself.
"Help me up," he said.
"You can help yourself when you've slept off your binge."
"I'm not drunk," Elof protested. "The fact is, as I started to run down the stairs, I thought I saw Big Ingmar coming toward me to take the watch. That's how I got such a nasty fall."

Then Halvor bent down and gave the poor wretch a lift, for his back was broken. He had to be put into a wagon and driven home. He would never again have the use of his legs. From that day on, Elof was confined to his bed, a helpless cripple. But he could talk, and all day long he kept begging for brandy. The doctor had left strict orders with Karin not to give him any spirits, lest he drink himself to death. So Elof tried to get what he wanted by shrieking and making the most hideous noises and swearing at everyone in the house.

That was Karin's most trying year. Her husband sometimes tormented her until it seemed she could not stand it any longer. The very air became polluted by his vile talk and profanity, so that the home was like a hell. Karin begged the Storms to keep little Ingmar with them during the holidays as well. She did not want her brother at home with her for a day, not even at Christmas.

All the servants at the Ingmar Farm were distantly related to the family and had always lived on the place. But for the feeling that they belonged to the Ingmarssons, they could not have gone on serving under such conditions. There were precious few nights they were allowed to sleep in peace. Elof was constantly devising new ways to torment both servants and Karin, to make them give in to his demands.
In this misery Karin passed a winter and a summer and another winter.

But Karin had a retreat to which she would flee at times, to be alone with her thoughts. Behind the hop garden there was a narrow seat upon which she often sat, with her elbows on her knees and her chin resting in her hands, staring straight ahead yet seeing nothing. In front of her were great stretches of cornfields, beyond which was the forest, and in the distance the range of hills and Mount Klack.

One evening in April she sat on her bench, feeling tired and listless, as one often does in the springtime when the snow turns to slush and the ground is still unwashed by spring rains. The hops lay sleeping under a cover of fir brush. Against the hills hung a thick mist, such as always accompanies a thaw. The birch tops were beginning to turn brown, but all along the edge of the forest there was still a deep border of snow. Spring would soon be there in earnest, and the thought of it made Karin sigh. "Another summer!" she murmured. "Another year of this miserable life! No end to it. No change, just sorrow and shame, day in and day out."
"I might better be dead," she sighed. "I seem to be here for no other purpose than to keep Elof from drinking himself to death."

Suddenly she looked up, as if she had heard someone calling her. Leaning against the hedge, looking straight at her, stood Halvor Halvorsson. She did not know when he had come, but apparently he had been standing there a good while.
"I thought I should find you over here," Halvor said.
"Oh, did you?"
"I remembered how in the old days you used to come here and sit and brood."
"I didn't have much to brood over at that time."
"Then your troubles were mostly imaginary."

Karin mused as she looked at Halvor: "He must be thinking what a fool I was not to have married him, such a handsome and dignified man. Now he's got me where he can gloat over me, and he has come only to laugh at me."
"I've been inside talking with Elof," Halvor explained. "It was really him I wanted to see."
Karin made no reply but sat there, rigid and unresponsive, her eyes on the ground and her hands crossed, prepared to meet all the scorn she expected Halvor would heap upon her.

"I said to him," Halvor continued, "that I considered myself largely to blame for his misfortune, since it was at my place that he got hurt." He paused a moment, as if waiting for some response from her, either approval or disapproval. But Karin was silent. "So I have asked him to come and live with me for a while. It would at least be a change, and he could see more people than he does here."
Then Karin raised her eyes, but otherwise remained as motionless as before.

"We have arranged to have him sent to my place tomorrow morning. I know he'll come, because he thinks he can get his liquor. But of course you must know, Karin, that that's out of the question. No indeed! It's no more to be had with me than with you. I shall expect him tomorrow. He is to have the little room off the shop, and I've promised him I'll leave his door open, so he can see everyone who comes and goes."
At Halvor's first words Karin wondered whether this was something he had made up. But gradually it dawned on her that he was in earnest.

In fact, Karin had always imagined that Halvor had courted her only for her money and connections. It had never occurred to her that he might have loved her for herself alone. She probably knew she was not the kind of girl that men cared for. Nor had she herself been in love, either with Halvor or Elof. But now that Halvor had come to her in her trouble and wanted to help, she was completely overwhelmed by the bigness of the man. She marveled that he could be so kind to the one who had wronged him. She could not grasp it. Her cold reserve gave way to a kind of quivering wonder.

Karin's heart began to beat violently and anxiously. She awoke to something she had never before experienced and wondered what it meant. Then all at once she realized that Halvor's kindness had thawed her frozen heart, and that love was beginning to flame up in her. Halvor went on explaining his plan, fearing all the while that she might oppose him. "It's hard for Elof too," he pleaded. "He needs a change of scene, and he won't make as much trouble for me as he has for you. It will be quite a different matter for me—a man who is in the shop all day, and who has many friends dropping in." He spoke quickly, with a kind of breathless anxiety, for Karin had turned very red and he thought she was angry.
Karin hardly knew what to do. She felt she could not move or say a word without letting Halvor see she was in love with him. Yet she knew she would have to give him some kind of answer.
Presently Halvor stopped talking and simply looked at her.
Then Karin rose, went up to him almost without thinking, and patted his hand. "God bless you, Halvor!" she said in a broken voice. "God bless you!"
Despite all her caution, Halvor must have sensed something, for he quickly grasped her hands and drew her to him.
"No! No!" she cried in alarm, freeing herself. Then she hurried away.
Elof had gone to live with Halvor. All summer he lay in the little bedroom off the shop. Halvor was not troubled with the care of him for long, for in the autumn he died.
Shortly after his death Mother Stina said to Halvor: "Now you must promise me one thing: promise me that you will be patient with Karin."
"Of course I'll be patient," Halvor returned, puzzled.
"She's someone worth winning, even if you have to wait seven long years."
But it was not so easy for Halvor to be patient, for he soon learned that one man after another was paying court to Karin. This began within a fortnight of Elof's funeral.

One Sunday afternoon Halvor sat on the steps in front of his shop, watching the people come and go. It occurred to him that an unusual number of fine rigs were moving in the direction of the Ingmar Farm. In the first carriage sat an inspector from Bergsana Foundry, in the second was the son of the proprietor of the Karmsund Inn, and last came the Magistrate Berger Sven Persson, who was the richest man in western Dalecarlia, and a sensible and highly esteemed man too. He was not yet fifty, and had recently become a widower.

When Halvor saw Berger Sven Persson driving by, he could not contain himself. He jumped to his feet and started down the road. In almost no time he was over the bridge and on the side of the river where the Ingmar Farm lay.

"I'd like to know where all those carriages have gone to," he said to himself. He followed the wheel ruts, half running, but becoming more and more determined. "I know this is stupid of me," he thought, remembering Mother Stina's warning. "But I'm only going as far as the gate, to see what they're up to down there."

In the best room at the Ingmars sat Berger Sven Persson and two other men, drinking coffee. Ingmar Ingmarsson, who still lived at the schoolhouse, was home for Sunday. He sat at table with them and acted as host, for Karin had excused herself, saying she had some work to do in the kitchen, as the maids had gone down to the mission house to hear the schoolmaster preach.

It was deadly dull in the parlor. All the men sat drinking their coffee without exchanging a word. The suitors were practically strangers to one another, and all three of them were watching for a chance to slip into the kitchen for a private word with Karin.
Presently the door opened and in stepped another caller, who was received by Ingmar and led to the table.
"This is Tims Halvor Halvorsson," said Ingmar, introducing the newcomer to Berger Sven Persson.
Sven Persson did not rise but greeted Halvor with a sweep of the hand, saying somewhat mockingly:
"It is a pleasure to meet so distinguished a personage."
Ingmar noisily drew up a chair for Halvor, so that he was spared the embarrassment of replying.

From the moment Halvor entered the room, all the suitors became chatty and began to boast. Each praised the others in turn. It was as if they had agreed to stand together until Halvor was well out of the running.
"The magistrate is driving a fine horse today," the inspector began.

Berger Sven Persson took up the game by complimenting the inspector on having shot a bear the winter before. Then the two turned to the innkeeper's son and said something in praise of a house his father was building.

Finally all three bragged about the wealth of Berger Sven Persson. They grew eloquent, and with every word they gave Halvor to understand that he was too lowly a man to think of competing with them. Halvor certainly did feel very insignificant, and bitterly regretted having come.

Just then Karin came along with fresh coffee. At the sight of Halvor she brightened for an instant. Then it occurred to her that his calling on her so soon after her husband's death looked rather bad. "If he is in such a hurry, people will surely say he hadn't given Elof proper care—that he wanted him out of the way so he could marry me." She would rather he had waited two or three years. That would have been long enough for people to see that he had not been impatient for Elof to die.

Everyone had stopped talking the moment Karin appeared, wondering how she and Halvor would greet each other. They barely touched hands. At which the magistrate expressed his delight with a short whistle, while the inspector broke into a loud guffaw. Halvor quietly turned to him. "What are you laughing at?" he said.
The inspector was at a loss for an answer. With Karin there, he did not wish to say anything offensive.
"He is thinking of a hound that raises a hare and lets someone else catch it," remarked the innkeeper's son with a smirk.

Karin turned blood red but refilled the coffee cups. "Berger Sven Persson and the rest of you will have to be satisfied with plain coffee," she said. "We no longer serve spirits to anyone on this farm."
"Nor do I at my home," said the magistrate approvingly.
The inspector and the innkeeper's son kept quiet. They understood that Sven Persson had scored heavily.

The magistrate at once began to hold forth on temperance and its benefits. Karin listened with interest and agreed with all he said. Seeing that this was the kind of talk that appealed to her, the magistrate began to spread himself. He delivered a long-winded speech on the curse of liquor and drunkenness. Karin recognized all her own thoughts on the subject, and was glad to find they were shared by so intelligent a man.
In the middle of his speech Berger Sven Persson glanced over at Halvor, who sat at the table looking glum and sulky, his coffee cup untouched.

"It's pretty rough on him," thought Berger Sven Persson, "particularly if there's any truth in what people say about his having given Elof a little push on his way into the next world. Anyway, he did Karin a good turn by relieving her of that dreadful drunkard." And since the magistrate felt he had as good as won the game, he felt rather friendly toward Halvor. Raising his cup, he said: "Here's to you, Halvor! You certainly did Karin a good turn when you took her drunken husband off her hands."
Halvor did not respond to the toast. He sat looking the man straight in the eye, wondering how to take this.
The inspector burst out laughing again. "Yes, yes, a good turn," he guffawed, "a real good turn."
"Yes, yes, a real good turn," echoed the innkeeper's son with a chuckle.

Before they were done laughing, Karin had vanished like a shadow through the kitchen door. But she could hear from the kitchen all that was said inside. She was both sorry and distressed over Halvor's untimely visit. It would probably mean she could never marry him. It was plain the gossips were already spreading evil reports. "I can't bear the thought of losing him," she sighed.
For a time no sound came from the sitting room, but presently she heard a noise as if a chair were being pushed back. Someone had evidently risen.
"Are you going already, Halvor?" young Ingmar was heard to say.
"Yes," Halvor replied. "I can't stay any longer. Please say goodbye to Karin for me."
"Why don't you go into the kitchen and say it yourself?"
"No," Halvor was heard to answer. "We two have nothing more to say to each other."

Karin's heart began to pump hard, and thoughts came rushing into her head as if on wings. Now Halvor was angry with her—and no wonder! She had hardly dared shake hands with him, and when the others scoffed at him, she never opened her mouth in his defense but quietly slipped away. Now he must think she did not care for him, and was therefore going, never to return. She could not understand why she had treated him so badly—she who was so fond of him. Then all at once her timidity and reserve seemed like sheer cowardice. "What are you afraid of?" she asked herself. "You who have stood by the bed of a drunkard these many years—are you going to knuckle under to a pack of gossipers?"
Karin hastily opened the door and stood facing Halvor before he could manage to leave the room.
"Are you leaving so soon, Halvor?" she asked. "I thought you were going to stay for supper."
Halvor stood staring at Karin. She seemed completely changed. Her cheeks were aglow, and there was something tender and appealing about her that he had never seen before.
"I'm going, and I'm not coming back," said Halvor. He had not caught her meaning, apparently.

"Do stay and finish your coffee," she urged. Then she took him by the hand and led him back to the table. She turned both white and red, and several times she nearly lost her courage. All the same she braved it out, though there was nothing she feared so much as scorn and contempt. "Now he will at least see that I'm willing to stand by him," she thought. Turning to the guests, she said: "Berger Sven Persson and all of you! Halvor and I have not spoken of this matter—I have so recently been widowed. But I want you to know that if there is any man in this parish I would consider marrying, that man is Halvor, who sits beside me here."
When Karin had finished speaking, she drew nearer to Halvor, as if seeking protection against all the cruel gossip that would come now.
The men were speechless, mostly from astonishment at Karin Ingmarsson, who looked younger and more girlish than ever before in her life.

Then Halvor said in a voice vibrant with feeling: "Karin, when I received your father's watch, I felt that nothing greater could have happened to me. But this thing you have just done surpasses everything."
Berger Sven Persson, who was in many ways an excellent man, arose.
"Let us all congratulate Karin and Halvor," he said graciously, "for everyone must know that he whom Karin, daughter of Ingmar, has chosen is a man of sterling worth."

chapters.title: Book Two — In Zion
paragraphs: That an old country schoolmaster should sometimes be a little too self-confident is not surprising. For nearly a lifetime he has been imparting knowledge and giving advice to his fellow men. He sees that a whole community is directed and guided by him, and naturally thinks himself a very important person. It is hard for him to imagine that there may come a time when the people will no longer listen to him.
One Sunday in winter, just after service, the pastor and the schoolmaster stood talking together in the vestry. The conversation had turned to the Salvation Army.
"It's a singular idea to have hit upon," the pastor remarked. "I never imagined I should live to see anything of that sort!"
The schoolmaster glanced sharply at the pastor. He thought the remark entirely irrelevant. Surely the pastor could never think that such an absurd innovation would find its way into their parish.
"I don't believe you are likely to see it, either," he said emphatically.
The pastor, knowing himself to be a weak and broken-down man, let the schoolmaster have things pretty much his own way. But all the same, he could not resist teasing him a little from time to time.

"How can you feel so certain that we shall escape the Salvation Army, Storm?" he said. "You see, when pastor and schoolmaster stand together, there's no danger of any nuisance of that sort crowding in."
To this the schoolmaster did not reply at once. Presently he said, quite meekly: "The pastor has never heard me preach."

The mission house was a sore point between them. The clergyman had never set foot in the place. And now that this touchy question had come up, both men were sorry they had said anything to hurt each other.
The little misunderstanding of the morning resulted in the pastor attending the schoolmaster's meeting that afternoon.
"I'll give Storm a pleasant surprise," he thought. "I will go to hear him preach in his Zion."

On the way to the mission house the pastor's thoughts went back to the time it was built. How full the air had been of prophecies, and how firmly he had believed that God had intended it to be something extraordinary—something far beyond what ordinary minds could conceive. But as one year after another had passed, and the only thing that happened was that the schoolmaster explained the Bible in his own solid but thoroughly orthodox way, the pastor had felt rather foolish for his enthusiasm.

The schoolmaster's Zion was a large hall with light-colored walls. On either side hung wood engravings of Luther and Melanchthon in fur-trimmed cloaks. Along the borders, close to the ceiling, ran a painted text: "Are your windows open toward Jerusalem?"

The large bare room was full of people, which was all that seemed necessary to create an atmosphere of impressive solemnity. Most of the people were dressed in the picturesque peasant costume of the province, their cheeks ruddy with the cold winter air. The women sat with their prayerbooks in their hands, the men with their legs stretched out, their arms folded, and their eyes half shut.
Storm had already begun his address when he saw the pastor come down the aisle and take a seat in the front row.
"You're a wonderful man, Storm!" the schoolmaster thought. "Everything comes your way. Here's the pastor himself to do you honor."

During the time the schoolmaster had been holding meetings, he had explained the Bible from cover to cover. That afternoon he spoke of the Heavenly Jerusalem and everlasting bliss, as described in the book of Revelation. He spoke so beautifully of the New Jerusalem with its gates of pearl and its streets of gold that many of his listeners felt as if they could actually see it. Some of them went so far as to say that the air in the room suddenly became fresh and sweet, like the air in a garden of roses.

The pastor became interested when the schoolmaster began to talk about Jerusalem. The strange misgivings he had had long ago flashed through his mind again. In the middle of the service the little girl Gertrude's words came back to him: "I have destroyed the parish in order to build a Jerusalem."
Storm had no sooner said "Amen" than a voice from the group by the door piped up: "I should very much like to say a few words."
"That must be Hoek Matts Ericsson," thought the pastor, and others with him. For no one else in the parish had such a sweet and childlike treble.
The next moment a little meek-faced man made his way up to the platform, followed by a score of men and women who seemed to be there to support and encourage him.

The pastor, the schoolmaster, and the entire congregation sat in suspense. "Hoek Matts has come to tell us of some awful calamity," they thought. "Either the king is dead, or war has been declared, or there is plague in the country."

"I want to say to the schoolmaster and to the congregation," he began, "that Sunday before last, while I was sitting at home with my family, the Spirit descended upon me and I began to preach. We could hardly believe it, but then it happened again, and now I feel impelled to come before this congregation."
Hoek Matts also said he was astonished that the gift of speech should have fallen upon so humble a man. "But the schoolmaster himself is only a peasant," he added, with a little more confidence.
After this preamble, Hoek Matts folded his hands and was ready to begin preaching at once. But by that time the schoolmaster had recovered from his first shock of surprise.
"Do you think of speaking here now, Hoek Matts—immediately?"

"Yes, that's my intention," the man replied. He grew as frightened as a child when Storm glowered at him. "It was my purpose, of course, to first ask leave of the schoolmaster and the rest," he stammered.
"We're all through for the day," said Storm conclusively.

Then the meek little man began to beg, his voice near tears: "Won't you please let me say a few words? I only want to tell of the things that have come to me when walking behind the plow and when working in the forest. Just a few words—"

But the schoolmaster, though he had had such a day of triumph himself, felt no pity for the poor little man. "Matts Ericsson comes here with his own peculiar notions, and claims they are messages from the Holy Spirit. Can I allow any such thing? Should I open the door to one of these false prophets for a single moment? In my meeting I shall have the true faith, and no other!" he thought.
Hoek Matts dared not protest, and the schoolmaster opened the hymnbook.

"Let us all join in singing hymn one hundred and eighty-seven," he said. He read out the hymn in stentorian tones, then began to sing at the top of his voice: "Are your windows open toward Jerusalem?"
Meanwhile he thought: "It was well after all that the pastor happened in today. Now he can see that I know how to maintain order in my Zion."

But no sooner was the hymn finished than a man jumped to his feet. It was the proud and dignified Ljung Bjoern Olafsson, who was married to one of the Ingmar girls and owned a large farmstead near the Ingmar Farm.
"We down at this end think the schoolmaster might have consulted our wishes before turning Matts Ericsson down," he mildly protested.
"Oh, you think so, do you, sonny?" The schoolmaster spoke in just the kind of tone he would have used in reproving some young upstart. "Then let me tell you that no one but myself has any say here."

Ljung Bjoern turned blood red. He had not meant to provoke a quarrel with Storm, but had simply wished to soften the blow for Hoek Matts, who was an inoffensive man. All the same, he could not help feeling riled.
"Twice I have heard Hoek Matts preach, and must say he is wonderful. I believe everyone present would benefit from hearing him."

The schoolmaster answered pleasantly enough, but in the old admonishing tone of the classroom: "Surely you understand, Krister Larsson, that I can't allow this. If I were to let Hoek Matts preach today, then tomorrow some Waldenstromian or Baptist might come along and demand the same privilege. Ah, no, my dear Krister!"
At this several people laughed. But Ljung Bjoern was ready with a sharp reply: "I see no reason why Krister and I shouldn't be as well qualified to preach as the schoolmaster," he said.

Tims Halvor arose and tried to calm them and prevent possible strife. "Those of us who have furnished the money to build and run this mission should be consulted before any new preacher is brought in. So let us drop the matter for today and discuss it at the next business meeting."

By that time Krister Larsson had become worked up and was on his feet again. "I recall that when we built this hall, we all agreed it should be a free-for-all meeting house and not a church where only one man can preach. My opinion is that the schoolmaster has no more right to refuse Matts Ericsson than any of the rest of us."

When Krister had spoken, everyone seemed to breathe easier. Only an hour before, it had not occurred to them that they could ever wish to hear any speaker but the schoolmaster. Now they thought it would be rather nice to hear Hoek Matts, who was said to be inspired by God. Faces began to light up and voices grew excited.

There would likely have been no further disturbance if only Bullet Gunner had stayed away that day. He too was a brother-in-law of Tims Halvor—a tall, gaunt fellow with a shifty and cunning look. He was rather ill-thought-of in the parish, for he was never disposed to lend a helping hand. But he was sharp and ready with his tongue.
"There was a lot of talk about freedom while we were building this house," said Gunner, "but I haven't heard a liberal word since the place first opened."

The schoolmaster grew purple. Gunner's remark was the first sign of actual hostility. "Let me remind you, Bullet Gunner, that here you have heard the true freedom preached, as Luther himself preached it. And you ought to be grateful to the man who has stood here for years and given you words of truth!"

"The schoolmaster would have us think that everything new is worthless as soon as it touches on doctrine," Gunner replied, half soothingly, half mockingly. "He approves of our using new methods of farming and new machines, but he won't let us hear a word of any new kind of preaching."
Storm began to think that Bullet Gunner's bark was worse than his bite. "Is it your meaning," he said in a jesting tone, "that we should preach a different doctrine here from the Lutheran?"
"It is not a question of a new doctrine," roared Gunner, "but of who shall preach! And as far as I know, Matts Ericsson is as good a Lutheran as either the schoolmaster or the parson."

For the moment the schoolmaster had forgotten about the parson. But now he glanced down at him. The clergyman sat quietly musing, his chin resting on the knob of his cane. There was a curious gleam in his eye and a faint smile on his lips.

"After all, perhaps it would have been just as well if the parson hadn't come today," thought the schoolmaster. What was happening reminded Storm of something he had experienced before. It felt like the start of all over again—the commotion over the mission house four years earlier. He decided he had heard enough.

Instantly there arose against him a perfect storm of protests. By that time everyone had become swollen with the idea that they were all just as good as the schoolmaster. "Why should he be the only one to preach? Were there not enough gifted men in the parish? It would be refreshing to hear a different voice."

These ideas seemed new to most of them, yet from the talk it was clear they had been germinating in their minds ever since the schoolmaster built the mission house and showed them that a plain peasant could stand up and speak the Word of God.

After a while Storm said to himself: "This tantrum must have spent itself by now. Time to show them who is master here." He rose, pounded the table with his fist, and, in a voice that could be heard across half the parish, shouted: "If there is nothing more to say, you will all go home now!"
Some of them actually did get up, for they had all gone to Storm's school and knew that when their teacher rapped on the table, everybody had to obey. Yet the majority stubbornly kept their seats.
"The schoolmaster forgets that now we are grown men," said one. "But he still seems to think we should jump just because he happens to rap on the table!" said another.

They went right on talking about wanting to hear new speakers, and which ones they should bring in. They were already quarreling among themselves as to whether it should be the Waldenstromians or the Baptists. Some were set on the Mission Friends, and others on the Methodists. But all were agreed on one thing: they wanted somebody new.

The schoolmaster stood staring at the crowd as if he were looking at some weird monstrosity. For until that moment he had seen only the child in each face. But now all the round baby cheeks had become angular and weather-beaten. The sleepy child eyes had turned quick and crafty. And the foolish little mouths had acquired a firm, hard set. These were not children but men—hard-headed peasants who were not to be controlled through fear. It was as if a century had passed in a single hour.

The tumult continued, growing louder and louder. The schoolmaster kept still and let them rage. Bullet Gunner, Ljung Bjoern, and Krister Larsson led the attack. Hoek Matts, who was the innocent cause of all the commotion, kept trying to silence them, but no one would listen to him.
Once again the schoolmaster glanced down at the parson, who was still quietly musing, the same gleam in his eyes, which were fixed on the schoolmaster.

"He's probably thinking of that evening four years ago when I told him I would build a mission," thought Storm. "He was right, too. Everything has turned out just as he said it would: heresy, revolt, disorder! And just now this could not have come at a worse time." But through all this self-reproach the schoolmaster saw one thing clearly: the mission house had been at fault from the very beginning. It had drawn the people away from the old road and onto a new one.

The instant this became clear to the schoolmaster, his head went up and his back straightened. He drew from his pocket a small key of polished steel. It was the key to Zion! He held it out to the congregation.
"Now I'm going to lay this key upon the table," he said, "and I shall never touch it again, for I see now that it has unlocked the door to everything I had hoped to shut out."
The schoolmaster put the key down, took up his hat, and walked straight over to the pastor.
"I want to thank you, Parson, for coming to hear me today," he said, "for if you hadn't come today, you never could have heard me."

chapters.title: Book Two — The Wild Hunt
paragraphs: There were many who thought Elof Ersson should have found no peace in his grave for the shameful way he had treated Karin and young Ingmar. He had deliberately squandered all of his and Karin's money, so she would suffer hardship after his death. He left the farm so heavily mortgaged that Karin would have been forced to turn it over to the creditors, had not Halvor been rich enough to buy the property and pay off the debts. Ingmar Ingmarsson's twenty thousand kroner, which Karin had intended to save for him, were also lost.

When Ingmar learned he was penniless, he consulted Karin about what he should do. He told his sister that of all things he would prefer to be a teacher, and begged her to let him remain with the Storms until he was old enough for college. Down at the village he would always be able to borrow books from the schoolmaster or the pastor, he said. Moreover, he could help Storm at the school by reading with the children. That would be excellent practice.
Karin turned this over in her mind before answering. "I suppose you wouldn't care to stay at home, since you can't become master here?" she said.

When Storm's daughter heard that Ingmar was coming back, she pulled a long face. It seemed to her that if they must have a boy living with them, they might better have the judge's good-looking son Bertil, or there was jolly Gabriel, the son of Hoek Matts Ericsson.

Gertrude liked both Gabriel and Bertil, but as for Ingmar, she couldn't exactly tell what her feelings were toward him. She liked him because he helped her with her lessons and minded her like a slave. But she could also become thoroughly annoyed with him sometimes, because he was clumsy and tiresome and did not know how to play. She had to admire his diligence and his knack for learning, yet at times she fairly despised him for not being able to show off what he could do.

Gertrude's head was always full of funny fancies and dreams, which she confided to Ingmar. If the lad happened to be away for a few days, she grew restless and felt she had no one to talk to. But as soon as he came back, she hardly knew what she had been longing for.

The girl had never thought of Ingmar as a boy of means and good family. She treated him rather as though he were a little beneath her. Yet when she heard Ingmar had become poor, she wept for him. And when he told her he would not try to get back his property, but meant to earn his own living as a teacher, she was so indignant she could hardly control herself.
The Lord only knows all she had dreamed he would be someday!

The children at Storm's school were given very strict training. They were held to their tasks, and only rarely allowed amusements. However, all this changed the spring Storm gave up his preaching. Mother Stina said to him: "Now, Storm, we must let the young folks be young. Remember that you and I were young once. Why, when we were seventeen, we danced many a night from sundown to sunup."
So one Saturday night, when young Gabriel and Gunhild, the councilman's daughter, came to visit the Storms, they actually had a dance at the schoolhouse.

Gertrude was wild with delight at being allowed to dance, but Ingmar would not join in. Instead he took up a book and sat down on the sofa by the window. Time and again Gertrude tried to make him put down his book, but Ingmar, sulky and shy, refused to budge. Mother Stina looked at him and shook her head. "It's plain he comes of an old, old stock," she thought. "That kind can never be truly young."
The three who did dance had such a good time! They talked of going to a proper dance the next Saturday evening, and asked the schoolmaster and Mother Stina what they thought.
"If you do your dancing at Strong Ingmar's, I give my consent," said Mother Stina, "for there you will meet only respectable folk."
Then Storm also made it conditional. "I can't allow Gertrude to go to a dance unless Ingmar goes along to look after her," he said.
All three rushed up to Ingmar and begged him to come.
"No!" he growled, without even glancing up from his book.

"It's no good asking him!" said Gertrude in a tone that made Ingmar raise his eyes. Gertrude looked radiantly beautiful after the dance. She smiled scornfully, and her eyes flashed as she turned away. It was plain how much she despised him for sitting there so ugly and sulky, like some crotchety old man. Ingmar had to change his mind and say yes—there was no way out of it.

A few evenings later, while Gertrude and Mother Stina sat spinning in the kitchen, the girl suddenly noticed her mother growing uneasy. Every little while she would stop her spinning wheel and listen. "I can't imagine what that noise is," she said. "Do you hear anything, Gertrude?"
"Yes, I do," the girl replied. "There must be someone upstairs in the classroom."
"Who could be there at this hour?" Mother Stina scoffed. "Only listen to the rustling and the pattering from one end of the room to the other!"
And there certainly was a rustling and a pattering and a bumping about over their heads that made both Gertrude and her mother feel uneasy.
"There must surely be someone up there," insisted Gertrude.
"There can't be," Mother Stina declared. "Let me tell you that this has been going on every night since you danced here."
Gertrude saw that her mother imagined the house had been haunted since the night of the dance. If that idea became fixed in Mother Stina's mind, there would be no more dancing for Gertrude.
"I'm going up there to see what it is," said the girl, rising. But her mother caught hold of her skirt.
"I don't know whether I dare let you go," she said.
"Nonsense, mother! It's best to find out what this is."
"Then I'd better go with you," the mother decided.
They crept softly up the stairs. When they got to the door they were afraid to open it. Mother Stina bent down and peeped through the keyhole. Presently she gave a little chuckle.
"What pleases you, mother?" asked Gertrude.
"See for yourself, only be very quiet!"

Then Gertrude put her eye to the keyhole. Inside, benches and desks had been pushed against the wall. In the center of the schoolroom, amid a cloud of dust, Ingmar Ingmarsson was whirling around with a chair in his arms.
"Has Ingmar gone mad!" exclaimed Gertrude.

"Shh!" warned the mother, drawing her away from the door and down the stairs. "He must be trying to teach himself to dance. I suppose he wants to learn so he'll be able to dance at the party," she added with a smirk. Then Mother Stina began to shake with laughter. "He came near frightening the life out of me," she admitted. "Thank God he can be young for once!" When she had gotten over her fit of laughing, she said: "You're not to say a word about this to anybody, do you hear!"

Saturday evening the four young people stood on the steps of the schoolhouse, ready to start. Mother Stina looked them over approvingly. The boys had on yellow buckskin breeches and green homespun waistcoats with bright red sleeves. Gunhild and Gertrude wore striped skirts bordered with red cloth and white blouses with big puffed sleeves. Flowered kerchiefs were crossed over their bodices, and they had on aprons that were as flowered as their kerchiefs.

As the four of them walked along in the twilight of a perfect spring evening, nothing was said for quite a long time. Now and then Gertrude would cast a side glance at Ingmar, thinking of how he had worked to learn to dance. Whether it was the memory of Ingmar's weird dancing or the anticipation of attending a real dance, her thoughts became light and airy. She managed to keep just a little behind the others so she could daydream undisturbed. She had made up a little story about the spring evening—about the trees being bare even though it was already warm.

It happened this way, she imagined: the trees, after sleeping peacefully the whole winter, suddenly began to dream. They dreamed that summer had come. They seemed to see the fields dressed in green grass and waving corn. The hawthorn shimmered with new-blown roses. Brooks and ponds were covered with water lily leaves. The stones were hidden under creeping tendrils, and the forest floor was thick with star flowers. And amid all this that was clothed in green, the trees alone stood naked.

In their confusion and embarrassment, the trees fancied that all the rest were making fun of them. The bumblebees came buzzing up to mock them. The magpies laughed them to scorn, while other birds sang taunting songs.
"Where shall we find something to put on?" the trees asked in despair. But they had not a leaf to their names on either twig or branch, and their distress was so terrible that it wakened them.
Glancing about, drowsy-like, their first thought was: "Thank God it was only a dream! There is certainly no summer here. It's lucky for us that we haven't overslept."

But as they looked around more carefully, they noticed the streams were clear of ice. Grass blades and crocuses peeped out from their beds of soil. Under their own bark the sap was running. "Spring is here at any rate," said the trees, "so it was well we woke. We have slept long enough for this year. Now it's high time we got dressed."

So the birches hurriedly put on some sticky pale green leaves, and the maples a few green flowers. The leaves of the alder came forth in such a crinkly and unfinished state that they looked quite misshapen. But the slender leaves of the willow slipped out of their buds smooth and shapely from the start.
Gertrude smiled to herself as she walked along and thought this up. She only wished she had been alone with Ingmar so she could have told it all to him.

They had a long way to go to reach the Ingmar Farm—more than an hour's walk. They followed the riverside. All the while Gertrude kept walking a little behind the others. Her fancy had begun to play around the red glow of the sunset, which flamed now above the river, now above the shore. Gray alder and green birch were wrapped in the shimmer, flashing red one instant, the next returning to their natural hues.
Suddenly Ingmar stopped and broke off in the middle of something he was saying.
"What's the matter, Ingmar?" asked Gunhild.

Ingmar, pale as a ghost, stood gazing at something in front of him. The others saw only a wide plain covered with grain fields and encircled by a range of hills, and in the center of the plain a big farmstead. At that moment the glow of sunset rested upon the farm. All the windowpanes glittered, and the old roofs and walls had a bright red shimmer about them.
Gertrude promptly stepped up to the others. After a quick glance at Ingmar, she drew Gunhild and Gabriel aside.

"We mustn't question him about anything around here," she said under her breath. "That place over there is the Ingmar Farm. The sight of it has probably made him sad. He hasn't been home in two years—not since he lost all his money."
The road they had taken was the one leading past the farm and down to Strong Ingmar's cabin at the edge of the forest.

Soon Ingmar came running after, calling, "Hadn't we better go this way instead?" Then he led them onto a path that wound around the edge of the forest, by which they could reach the cabin without crossing the farm itself.
"You know Strong Ingmar, I suppose?" said Gabriel.
"Oh, yes," young Ingmar replied. "We used to be good friends in the old days."
"Is it true that he understands magic?" asked Gunhild.
"Well—no!" Ingmar answered rather hesitantly, as if half believing it himself.
"You may as well tell us what you know," Gunhild persisted.
"The schoolmaster says we mustn't believe in such things."
"The schoolmaster can't prevent a person seeing what he sees and believing what he knows," Gabriel declared.

Ingmar wanted to tell them all about his home. Memories of his childhood came back at the sight of the old place. "I can tell you about something I saw once," he said. "It happened one winter when father and Strong Ingmar were up in the forest working at the kiln. When Christmas came round, Strong Ingmar offered to tend the kiln by himself, so father could come home for the holidays. The day before Christmas, mother sent me up to the forest with a basket of good food for Strong Ingmar."

"Soon father came in laughing. He and the old man were black with soot and reeking with the smell of sour charcoal smoke. But never had I seen father so happy and full of fun. Neither of them could stand upright in the hut, and the only furniture was two bunks made of spruce twigs and a couple of flat stones on which they had built a fire. Yet they were perfectly content. They sat down side by side on one of the bunks and opened the basket. 'I don't know whether you can have any of this,' said father. 'It was sent to Strong Ingmar.' 'Well, it looks as though your mother meant it for both of us,' said the old man; 'she has certainly put in enough for two.'"

"They carried on like that the whole time they were eating. Mother had sent a little brandy along with the food. I marveled that people could be so happy over food and drink. 'You'll have to tell your mother that Big Ingmar has eaten up everything,' said the old man, 'and that she will have to send more tomorrow.' 'So I see,' said I."

"Just then I was startled by a crackling noise in the fireplace. It sounded as if someone had cast a handful of pebbles on the stones. Father did not notice it, but at once Strong Ingmar said: 'What, so soon?' Yet he went on eating. Then there was more crackling, much louder. Now it sounded as if a shovelful of stones had been thrown on the fire. 'Well, well, is it so urgent!' Strong Ingmar exclaimed. Then he went out. 'The charcoal must be on fire!' he shouted back. 'Just you sit still and I'll tend to it.' He was gone quite a while, and father and I finished our eating."

"After a while Strong Ingmar returned, and the fun began again. 'I haven't had such a merry Christmas in years,' he laughed. He had no sooner gotten the words out of his mouth than the crackling started up again. 'What, again? Well, I never!' And out he flew in a flash. The charcoal was on fire again. When the old man came back for the second time, father said to him: 'I see you have such good help up here that you can manage by yourself.' 'Yes, you can safely go home and keep your Christmas,' Strong Ingmar replied."

Gunhild thanked Ingmar for his story, but Gertrude walked on in silence, as if she had become frightened. It was beginning to get dark. Everything that had looked so rosy a while ago was now either blue or gray. Here and there in the forest could be seen a shiny leaf that gleamed in the twilight like the red eye of a troll.

Gertrude was astonished at Ingmar having talked so much and so long. He seemed like a different person since coming onto home ground. He carried his head higher than usual and stepped with firmer tread. Gertrude did not quite like this change in him. It made her uneasy. All the same she plucked up her courage and began to tease Ingmar about coming home to dance.

Then at last they came to a little gray hut. Candles were burning inside, the windows being too small to let in much light. They caught the sound of violin music and the clatter of dancing feet. Still the girls paused, wondering. "Is it here?" they questioned. "Can anyone dance here? The place looks too small to hold even one couple."
"Go on inside," said Gabriel. "The hut isn't as tiny as it looks."

Outside the door, which was open, stood a group of boys and girls who had danced themselves into a warm glow. The girls were fanning themselves with their headshawls, and the boys had pulled off their short black jackets to dance in their bright green red-sleeved waistcoats.
The newcomers edged their way through the crowd by the door into the hut. The first person they saw was Strong Ingmar—a little fat man with a big head and a long beard.
"He must be related to the elves and the trolls," thought Gertrude. The old man was standing on the hearth, playing his fiddle, so as not to be in the way of the dancers.

The hut was larger than it had appeared from outside, but it looked poor and dilapidated. The bare pine walls were worm-eaten, and the beams were blackened by smoke. There were no curtains at the windows and no cover on the table. It was clear that Strong Ingmar lived by himself. His children had all left him and gone to America. The only pleasure the old man had in his loneliness was to gather the young folks around him on a Saturday evening and let them dance to his fiddle.

It was dim in the hut and suffocatingly close. Couple after couple were whirling about in there. Gertrude could scarcely breathe and wanted to hurry out again, but it was impossible to get past the tight wedge of people blocking the doorway.

Strong Ingmar played with a sure stroke and in perfect time, but the instant young Ingmarsson came into the room he drew his bow across the strings, making a rasping noise that brought all the dancers to a halt. "It's nothing," he shouted. "Go on with the dance!"

Ingmar put his arm around Gertrude's waist to dance out the figure. Gertrude seemed very surprised that he wanted to dance. But they could get nowhere, for the dancers followed each other so closely that no one who had not been there from the start could squeeze in between them.
The old man stopped short, rapped on the fender with his bow, and said in a commanding voice: "Room must be made for Big Ingmar's son when there's any dancing in my house!"
With that everyone turned to have a look at Ingmar, who became so embarrassed that he could not stir. Gertrude had to take hold of him and practically drag him across the floor.

As soon as the dance was finished, the fiddler came down to greet Ingmar. When he felt Ingmar's hand in his, the old man pretended to be very concerned and instantly let go. "My goodness!" he exclaimed. "Be careful of those delicate schoolmaster hands! A clumsy old fellow like me could easily crush them."

He took young Ingmar and his friends up to the table, driving away several old women who were sitting there looking on. Then he went over to the cupboard and brought out some bread and butter and root beer.
"I don't usually offer refreshments at these affairs," he said. "The others have to be content with just music and dancing. But Ingmar Ingmarsson must have a bite to eat under my roof."
Drawing up a little three-legged stool, the old man sat down in front of Ingmar and looked sharply at him.
"So you're going to be a schoolteacher, eh?" he asked.
Ingmar closed his eyes for a moment. There was the shadow of a smile on his lips, but all the same he answered rather sadly: "They have no use for me at home."
"No use for you?" cried the old man. "You don't know how soon you may be needed on the farm. Elof lived only two years, and who knows how long Halvor will hold out?"
"Halvor is a strong, healthy fellow," Ingmar pointed out.
"You must know, of course, that Halvor will turn the farm over to you as soon as you're able to buy it back."
"He'd be a fool to give up the Ingmar Farm now that it has fallen into his hands."

During this exchange Ingmar sat gripping the edge of the plain deal table. Suddenly a noise was heard as of something cracking. Ingmar had broken off a corner of the table. "If you become a schoolteacher, he'll never let you have the farm," the old man went on.
"You think not?"
"Think—think? Well, it's plain how you have been brought up. Have you ever driven a plow?"
"No."
"Or tended a kiln, or felled a huge pine?"
Ingmar sat there looking quite calm, but the table kept crumbling under his fingers. Finally the old man began to take notice.

"See here, young man!" he said when he saw what was happening. "I shall have to take you in hand again." Then he picked up some of the splinters and tried to fit them back into place. "You rogue! You ought to be going around to fairs, showing your tricks for money!" he laughed. Dealing Ingmar a hard whack on the shoulder, he remarked: "Oh, you'd make a fine schoolteacher, you would!"

In a flash he was back at the fireplace, fiddling away. Now there was a snap and a drive to his playing. He beat time with his foot and set the dancers whirling. "This is young Ingmar's polka," he called out. "Hoop-la! Now the whole house must dance for young Ingmar!"

Two such pretty girls as Gertrude and Gunhild had to be in every dance, of course. Ingmar did not dance much. He stood talking most of the time with some of the older men at the far end of the room. Between dances the people crowded around him as if it did them good just to look at him.

Gertrude thought Ingmar had entirely forgotten her, which made her quite miserable. "Now he feels he is the son of Big Ingmar, and that I am only the schoolmaster's Gertrude," she pouted. It seemed strange that she should take this so to heart. Between dances some of the young folk went out for a breath of air. The night had grown piercingly cold. It was quite dark, and since no one wanted to go home, they all said: "We'd better wait a little while. The moon will soon be out. Then it won't be so dark on the way home."

Once, when Ingmar and Gertrude happened to be standing outside the door, the old man came and drew the boy away. "Come, let me show you something," he said. Taking Ingmar by the hand, he led him through a thicket a short distance from the house. "Stand still now and look down!" he said. Ingmar found himself looking down a cleft, at the bottom of which something white shimmered. "This must be Langfors Rapids," said young Ingmar.
"Right you are," nodded the old man. "Now what do you suppose a waterfall like that can be used for, eh?"
"It might be used to run a mill," said Ingmar thoughtfully.

The old man laughed to himself. He patted Ingmar on the back, then gave him a dig in the ribs that almost sent him into the rapids. "But who's going to put up a mill here? Who's going to get rich, and who's going to buy the Ingmar Farm, eh?" he chuckled.
"I'd just like to know," said Ingmar.

Then the old man began unfolding a big plan he had in mind. Ingmar was to persuade Tims Halvor to put up a sawmill below the rapids, and then lease it to him. For many years the old man's dream had been to find a way for Big Ingmar's son to come into his own again. Ingmar stood quietly looking down at the foaming rapids.

"Come, let's go back to the house and the dancing!" said the old man. But as Ingmar did not move, he waited patiently. "If he's the right sort, he won't answer today, or tomorrow," he said to himself. "An Ingmarsson has to have time to think things over."
And as they stood there, all at once they heard a sharp, angry bark that seemed to come from some dog running loose in the forest.
"Do you hear that, Ingmar?" asked the old man.
"Yes. That must be a dog on the loose."
